Manuscript: Manuscript 4826, Śrī Raghunātha Temple MSS Library, Jammu. Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Anirban Dash. Diplomatic transcription of the manuscript. Revision 0: November 21, 2023. Country of publication: India.
Tripurabhairavīpañcāṅga, No.
Title: Tripurabhairavī Pañcāṅga from the Rudrayāmala Tantra. Author: [Not specified]. Folio number: 55. Total folios: 55.
Subject: The Five-limbed Ritual Manual (Pañcāṅga) of Tripurabhairavī, from the Viśvasāroddhāra, folio 1a:
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Tripurabhairavī; she who destroys the darkness of ignorance.
May the Tripura-mahātejas—the seed of bliss, inconceivable, and the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra—descend [upon us].
Or rather, I shall now declare the supreme Vidyā, the Tripurā, which is most well-guarded; by knowing which, one becomes the sovereign of the hosts of Siddhas.
That syllable consists of *ra*, *vi*, *kha*, *bhṛgu* (4), *hutāśa* (3), *stha* (8), *bhautika* (5), *bindu-śekhara* (the nasal dot);
it is situated in the directions of *kim*, *yat*, *tat*, etc., and in the positions of Indra (1) and Agni (3), possessing the eye (*akṣi*) and the dot (*bindu*);
it is situated in *ākāśa* (0), *bhṛgu* (4), and *vahni* (3), and is the mantra of creation with the moon (*indu*).
The syllable *khaṃḍavān* is the first seed (*vāgbhava*), the second is the *kāmarāja*,
and the third is known as the *śakti* seed; this Vidyā, consisting of five peaks (*pañcakūṭātmikā*) and proclaimed through these three seeds, is the *Tripurā-vidyā*.
Bhairavī is the seer (ṛṣi), Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the sage, and Paṅkti is declared to be the meter; the deity is said by the teachers to be the goddess Tripurabhairavī.
Her mantra, beginning with the syllable Vāgbhava, extends from the navel down to the feet.
Furthermore, one should place the seed-syllable of Kāma from the heart down to the navel;
one should place the third [syllable] from the head down to the region of the heart;
and again, the first and second [syllables] on the two hands, and the third... [on the feet].
One should place [the seed-syllables] on the head and the foundation (ādhāra); having placed them again on the heart,
one should perform the nine-yoni nyāsa in sequence with the three seed-syllables, and then again on the two ears and the chin.
One should again place [the letters] in the two conch-shells, in the mouth, in the two eyes,
in the two nostrils, in the belly, then in the two elbows, in the two sides of the abdomen,
in the two knees, in the head, in the two feet, in the private parts, and in the two flanks.

One should place [the syllables] in the heart-lotus, the two breasts, the region of the throat, and so forth; one should perform the placement (nyāsa) with the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) of *Rati* in the heart, *Prīti* between the eyebrows, and *Manobhava* in the head.
In these [mantras], one should place [the goddesses] Amṛteśī, Viśveśī,
and Viśvayoni in reverse order; one should perform the placement on the head (mūrdhanyāsa) using the seed-syllables in reverse order, beginning with their respective seed-syllables.

The knower of the Self should place Īśāna on the head, Manobhava (the mind-born) on the face, Tatpuruṣa on the heart, and Makaradhvaja; thereafter, he should place Ghorakumāra and others, and Kandarpa in the secret region, along with Vāmadeva.

Then, one should place Dimanmatha and Sadyojātakāmadeva at the two feet; subsequently, having placed those [deities] in the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western faces as before, [one places] Bhṛgu and Vyoman.
The seed-syllable of these is proclaimed as *e* with the five short vowels from *a* onwards arranged in pairs.
The ritual of the limbs (*aṅgakriyā*) is considered to be performed with the first seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels.
The practitioner should place the five arrows upon the breasts. The mantra is *trailokyamohana*.
One should worship Kyāmohanī with the two syllables *drā*, Drāviṇī on the head with the two syllables *drī*,
Kṣobhaṇī at the feet, Vaśīkaraṇī on the head preceded by the seed-syllable *klīṃ*,
and Ākarṣaṇī at the heart preceded by the seed-syllable *klīṃ*.

This placement of the arrows (*bāṇanyāsa*) has been described in sequence as being joined with the *Na-sarga* (ṅa) and *Bhṛgu* (ma), which is the "deluding" (*saṃmohanī*) [mantra]. It is to be placed on the forehead, between the eyebrows,
the mouth, the throat, the heart, and the navel.
On the two [sides] of page 2b), the five Tārās and the Subhagā group are to be installed by the mantra-practitioner according to the rite: first Subhagā, then Bhagā, Bhagamarpī,
followed by Parābhagamālinī, and after that Anaṅgā and Anaṅga.

Furthermore, there were Anaṅgamekhalās who had become like flowers, and Anaṅgamadanas who were languid with the intoxication of universal passion; they were adorned with the colors and ornaments of the principal deities, and held rosaries and water-pots.
With lotus-like hands granting fearlessness and boons, and with the syllables *vāk* (aiṃ),
*kāmaḥ* (klīṃ), *blū*, *strī* (hrīṃ), and *sauḥ*, these five Tārās have been proclaimed;
the best of practitioners, desiring prosperity, should perform this placement known as the "Ornament" (*bhūṣaṇa*).
One should place the vowels in the head, forehead, eyebrows, pair of ears, eyes, nose, cheeks, lips,
rows of teeth, and mouth; and [the consonants] in the chin,
throat, neck, sides, and pair of breasts.

One who is not composed should place the letters beginning with *ka* in these locations: the two armpits, the two elbows, the two hands, the region of their backs, the navel, the secret organ, and again on the thighs, knees, and the two shins.
(Page 3a)

The best of teachers should thus place these eight [mudrās]: the *kaṭyāgra* on the hips, the *kaṇṭhagra* on the neck, the *kaṭaka* behind, the *hṛdaya* on the heart, the *guhyaka* on the private parts, the *karṇakuṇḍala* on the two ears, the *mauli* on the head, the *lavaḍa* on the eyes, and the *sākṣaśīrṣaka* on the top of the head. Thus [he should proceed].
Having cast off the body, one should meditate upon Tripurabhairavī: *Oṃ*, she whose splendor is like that of a thousand rising suns, who wears a saffron silk garment and a garland on her head,
whose breasts are smeared with red pigment, and who holds a rosary, a book, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I bow to the Goddess who holds excellent boons in her lotus-like hands, whose lotus-face possesses the beauty of three eyes, who wears a crown of jewels and the cool-rayed moon,
and who smiles gently; having received initiation, one should recite the mantra while keeping the reality as the object of focus, with the senses conquered.

The seeker of power (*driyaḥ*) should offer thousands of flowers born from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), or flowers produced from the *karavīra*. Or, one may offer a lotus endowed with eight petals, its pericarp enriched with a new *yoni*. This is for the sake of [fulfilling] desires.

One should worship the seat of Bhairavī, joined with the powers of the directions: first Icchā (Will), then Jñānā (Knowledge), Kriyā (Action), Kāmanī (the Desirable), Kāmadāyinī (the Bestower of Desires),
Ratī (Delight), Rati-priyā (Beloved of Delight), Ānandā (Bliss), Manonmanī (Beyond Mind), and Varadā (the Giver of Boons).
If the nine Śaktis of Āriṇī are proclaimed: Vāgbhava, Lohita, Rāya, Śrīkaṇṭha, Lohita, Nala, Dīrgha, Vāṇī;
then Parā, followed by Aparā, Ha-Sauṃ, and again Sadāśiva Mahāpre.
"Obeisance to that very lotus-seat"— with this mantra, one should offer the seat of the venerable Kurukrama; one should worship in the space between the east and the center,
and then, by means of five *praṇavas*, one should fashion the form within it.
One should worship the external deity with a concentrated mind according to the procedure taught in the Āgamas.
[With] five *praṇavas*, the mantra is remembered as *tāra-vāk-vaktrikamala-ha-sa-kha-phreṃ-hasau*; one should worship in the left corner.
One should visualize the goddess Prīti, whose radiance is like that of the moon, holding a bow and a noose,
overwhelmed by the intoxication of passion, resembling molten gold, and stationed in the southern corner, holding a goad and a gesture of salutation with her two hands.
One should worship her first, holding the *dhāraṇī*, as the Mind-born Goddess (*Manobhavā*), red in color, adorned with red flowers and other ornaments, holding a sugarcane bow and flower-arrows,
with a smiling countenance; thereafter, one should worship her limbs as before.
The knower of the *dhānas* should worship those goddesses of Bāṇa with mantras that cause the flow of the tip of the *ikṣu*;
with lotus-hands holding flowers, they are radiant with prostrations.
One should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Subhagā, within the eight *yoni*s.
One should duly worship Madhu, Uśīra, and Bhairava, who are situated on the lap [of the Goddess] and are overwhelmed by the play of passion,
upon the eight petals with flowers and other offerings; then, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in those directions and their weapons outside of them.
Having recognized her as the Supreme Deity through merits accumulated over many births, he who unites with her according to the prescribed path shall become the abode of all prosperity.
Once the mantra is thus mastered, the practitioner should accomplish his own desired goal; he should offer oblations of red flowers.

Every day, one should feed twice as many or half that number of Brahmins with faultless foods soaked in honey; one should gratify beautiful young women with the thought that they are deities, and at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), one should satisfy them with wealth, grain, and other gifts.
One should praise one's own guru; when this is done, the world becomes submissive and the abode of Rāmā shall come to be.
With red lotuses smeared with the three sweets, with red flowers from the Aruṇa forest, and with milk-offerings mixed with ghee, one should perform the oblation.
The practitioner shall bring the entire universe under his control and attain mastery over speech.
By offering palāśa flowers mixed with camphor and aguru, the subduer shall obtain divine knowledge; by that very means, he shall become successful in the assembly.
The poet knows that an oblation of pieces of *amṛtā* smeared with milk conquers all untimely death;
an oblation of *dūrvā* grass smeared with milk for three days grants longevity; and one who offers flowers from the *kṣīrikarṇa* tree brings the Brahmins under one's influence.

By offering *kalhāra* flowers, one subdues kings; by offering *karṇikāra* flowers, one’s wife; and by offering *mallikā* flowers, one brings princes under one's control. By offering *koraṇḍu* flowers, one subdues courtesans; and by *pāṭala* flowers, one subdues *vṛṣalas*.
Having recited the mantra— which contains the name of the target (sādhya) situated within the forward and reverse orders of the seed-syllables—
the practitioner should offer oblations of sweet and red mustard seeds mixed with honey; in an instant, he shall bring kings under his control.

By this very procedure, one will certainly bring under control through oblation his wife and even his sons, as well as men, women, and kings, using flowers produced from the *mālatī* and *vakula* trees, combined with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*).

With those flowers and red sandalwood, one should perform oblations; within a year, one obtains poetic skill and the three mantras. With fruits produced from the *bilva* tree combined with the three sweets (*madhuratrika*), one should perform oblations; one will bring the worlds and prosperity under one's control.

He who offers oblations with blossoming *pāṭala*, *kumuda*, *kunda*, *utpala*, *nāga-campaka*, and *nandyāvarta* flowers arranged as garlands, attains his desired goal within a year; his ritual action bears fruit before that time.
One who has conquered the earthly realm should offer oblations of food mixed with clarified butter; he shall become prosperous in food.
One should offer camphor combined with musk and saffron to subjugate others; such a person immediately attains good fortune that surpasses even that of Kandarpa.
The practitioner of mantras should offer parched grain (lājā) soaked in curd, milk, and honey as oblations;
having thus conquered all diseases, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
[One part] of sandalwood, one part of saffron stamens, and one part of gorocanā.
One should grind these three together with snow-water and apply them as a tilaka;
from the Bhāleya [mountain], it is seen on the side today that as long as one touches it,
those who are touched will become helpless, and for a long time they will be like camphor.

One should prepare equal parts of *caurāṇi*. One-fourth part is considered to be *jaṭāmāṃsī*, and the same amount is considered to be *rocanā*. Saffron (*kuṅkuma*) should be seven parts, and sandalwood (*candana*) is considered to be two parts. *Aguru* should be nine parts.
And by this sequence of one-sixteenth parts, even a maiden [is purified] with snow-water;
all this has been well established. Taking the *tilaka* mark on her forehead, she should [subdue] kings and men who are arrogant with the pride of women.

By the mere sight of this tilaka, which contains the syllable *ḍhyāṃ* in its center and consists of nine [syllables], one shall surely subdue intoxicated elephants, lions, tigers, great serpents, bhūtas, vetālas,
and rākṣasas.
One should scratch out the seed-syllables, which are the letters of the three Gāyatrīs; then,

having written them again within the openings of the eight petals, it is surrounded by the alphabet (mātṛkā), enclosed by two layers of earth-elements (bhūbimba), and wound around the corners with the Manmatha-mantra.
This yantra is declared to be that of Tripura, which agitates the three worlds and bestows the state of Śrī.
Having invoked the deity into this yantra and worshipped her with oblations,
one should prepare a mixture of lac and the three metals.
This yantra, when held in the arm, brings victory in battles; it shall grant victory in debate and bestow abundant poetic skill. It increases longevity, health, friends, sons, and grandsons.
One should first write this [mantra] in the center of a hexagon; then,
subsequently, in the six corners and in the eight petals,
it should be surrounded externally by the seed-syllable of space (the letter *Ha*) and the earth-syllable (*La*).

This yantra, which bestows good fortune, prosperity, and the attainment of poetry and fame, is said to be drawn with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) on the petals and the pericarp located within the circle. (Page 6b)

One should write the *Vāgbhava* (AIM) syllable within the triangle situated between the two houses of Fire; then, one should draw the syllable *DHŪM* at the junctions of the six corners and encircle it with the *Strīkṣaṇa* (HRĪM) as prescribed.
This *tripura* yantra, which agitates the mind of the three worlds, consists of five *manobhava*s (Kāmas) and bestows the wealth of beauty.
The first [syllable] has a bindu at its base and is situated upon Brahmā and Indra, joined with the Moon; this is the second.
Manu, enriched by the lineage of Bhṛgu, proclaimed this third [mantra],
which is renowned as "Eṣa Vālā" and brings the three worlds under its control;
one should perform all its recitation, worship, and other rites as previously described.
One should recite the word "mānmathatripurādevi vidmahe," then utter the word "utkāmeśvari dhīmahi," and after that,
one should further say "tanno klinne pracodayāt. This is the Gāyatrī.
This *Tripurī* has been fully described as the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). O *Tripura*, having praised you with this [hymn], may you grant the attainment of desired fruits.
May those humans and gods who worship you attain that prosperity which is honored by men and demigods.

Thus ends the Chapter on Śrī Tripurabhairavī. Oṃ, salutations to the Śrī Devī. Oṃ, thereupon the illustrious practitioner, having risen from his bed during the auspicious hour of Brahmā (brāhma-muhūrta), having washed his hands and feet, and having sat down upon his own seat—
Upon the moon-maṇḍala within the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus of white color on the crown of one's own head,
[one should meditate upon] one's own guru, white in color and adorned with white ornaments, [possessing] wisdom...
He whose mind is blissful and joyful, whose form is pure consciousness and bliss, who has three eyes and four arms, who holds the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*), a book,
and the gestures of boon (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*) in his hands, and who holds a lotus in his left hand on his left side.

Having meditated upon the Supreme Śiva— the primordial deity of all deities, peaceful, gracious, and tranquil— who is embraced with his right arm by her who wears red garments and ornaments according to her own capacity, [one should worship] at his feet...
Visualizing oneself as bathed by the stream of nectar flowing from the pair of breasts, one should worship with mental offerings,
[saying]: "I offer fragrance consisting of the earth element."

*Namaḥ*. Having worshipped the flower whose essence is *haṃ* (space), the incense whose essence is *yaṃ* (wind), the lamp whose essence is *raṃ* (fire), and the various offerings such as food, fruit, roots, and betel whose essences are *vaṃ* (nectar) and *saṃ* (the universal soul), [one recites]: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hasa*.
KHAPHREṂ HASARAKṢAMALAVAYŪṂSAH KHAPHREṂ HASARAKṢAMALAVARAYA ŪṂ HSAUṂ SHAUḤ ŚRĪMACCHRĪ AMUKĀNANDANĀTHA-ŚRĪPĀDUKĀṂ ŚRĪŚIVĀMBĀM.

Having recited "I worship the sandals, obeisance" ten times, one should perform a prostration with the staff (lying flat on the ground) while mentally repeating it. In that regard, the mantras for prostration are as follows: *Oṃ namāmi sadgurum*.

For the sake of attaining the goals of liberation, desire, and wealth, I bow my head to the venerable Guru, the embodiment of supreme bliss, whose form is peace, who is directly manifest as Śiva, and who resides upon the seat of the crown of the head.
1. I shall worship the venerable Guru, the supreme bliss, whose very body is bliss.

Salutation to that venerable Guru by whose mere presence supreme consciousness-bliss arises, by whom that state has been revealed— the state which is of the form of an indivisible sphere and by which the moving and unmoving world is pervaded. (2-3)
To him whose eyes were opened by the stone of knowledge for one blinded by the cataract of ignorance—
salutations to that glorious Guru, who is Brahmā, who is Viṣṇu, and who is Maheśvara himself.

*Raḥ*. To Him alone who is the entire universe, to that venerable Śiva in the form of the Guru, who has assumed manifold forms for the sake of perfecting the descent of knowledge—to Him, the illustrious one, obeisance. *Namaḥ*.
To that Lord, the venerable Śiva in the form of the Guru... [for the sake of the successful manifestation of wisdom]. *Svīkṛtānekavi...* [who has accepted many...]

Salutations to the Supreme Self, who is independent, whose form is fashioned by compassion, who is the sole embodiment of ultimate reality, who takes the form of the nine planets and the two solstices, who is the sun that destroys the darkness of all ignorance, and who is a mass of pure consciousness.

For the sake of devotion for those who are not dependent on others; for the sake of existence for those who are destined for liberation (*bhavya*); for the sake of discernment for the discerning; for the sake of investigation for those who investigate;
for the sake of illumination for the luminous; and for the sake of knowledge for the knowers. (p. 8b) For the sake of knowledge for the knowers.
One should pay homage to the embodied one in front, at the sides,
behind, above, and below— whether manifest or unmanifest— in whatever form he may be; thus, having prostrated before the venerable Guru...
Having visualized [the deity] with a serene mind and received his command,
[one should contemplate him] within the triangular wheel situated at the center of the pericarp of the four-petalled golden lotus in the *mūlādhāra*.

Upon that *śṛṅgāṭaka*, one should contemplate the supreme power, Kuṇḍalinī, radiant as a thousand rising suns, possessing the luster of ten million flashes of lightning, the mother of all mantras, and the source of all.

[One should meditate upon] the life-force of living beings, whose abode is the three abodes, who has the form of a serpent with her face turned upwards, who possesses three and a half coils, whose face is directed upward, who is as slender as a lotus fiber, and whose body consists of the fifty letters. Eight...
Having meditated upon the dream-state as consisting of thirty *kalās*, and having awakened it by means of one's own innate *nāda* as instructed by the Guru,
[one should place] *vaṃ namaḥ*, *śaṃ*, *ṣaṃ*, and *saṃ* upon those four petals.
Having thus worshipped [the deities] upon the petals, in the center, and at the base in a clockwise direction, and having raised them up from all sides with the mantra *haṃ si*,
one should lead the lotus from the *kāmakalā* and then [proceed] with *svā*.
Having brought you to the six-petaled lotus, coral-colored, at the base of the *liṅga* in the place of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*),
[worship] there with "vaṃ namaḥ," and on the petals and in the center with "bhaṃ," "maṃ," "yaṃ," "raṃ," "laṃ," and the root mantra.
Having worshipped [the deity], one should then lead them by means of the *maṇipūra* [cakra]— which is blue in color and has ten petals— to that place where the *duṃbha* syllables are located:
*ḍaṃ*, *ḍhaṃ*, *ṇaṃ*, *taṃ*, *thaṃ*, *daṃ*, *dhaṃ*, *naṃ*, *paṃ*, *phaṃ*.
Having thus worshipped her at the root within the midst of the mantras,
one should then lead her to the twelve-petaled lotus in the *anāhata* cakra at the heart, which is of a reddish-brown (*piṅgala*) color;
there, [one worships] *kaṃ namaḥ*, *khaṃ*, *gaṃ*, *ghaṃ*.
Having worshipped with the root mantra in the center of the petals [inscribed with] Ṅaṃ, Caṃ, Chaṃ, Jaṃ, Jhaṃ, Ñaṃ, Ṭaṃ, and Ṭhaṃ, one should then lead her to the Viśuddhi-cakra,
a sixteen-petaled lotus of smoky color.

Therein: *aṃ namaḥ*, *āṃ*, *iṃ*, *ī*, *uṃ*, *ūṃ*, *ṛṃ*, *ṝṃ*, *ḷṃ*, *ḹṃ*, *eṃ*, *aiṃ*, *oṃ*, *auṃ*, *aṃ*, *aḥ*. Having worshipped these in the center of the leaf of the ascetic with the root mantra, one should then [worship] the Ājñā [cakra] between the eyebrows.
Having brought that [lotus] which has the color of lightning and two petals,
one should worship there with "Oṃ Namaḥ" and "Kṣaṃ Namaḥ" upon the petals and the center by means of the root-mantra; thereafter, the thousand-petaled lotus.
Having attained oneness with the Supreme Śiva, who consists of light in the form of the bindu situated within the *karṇikā*, one should satisfy [the deities] with the nectar flowing from him,
and there listen to the *nāda*.
(p. 10a) Having meditated on their dissolution for a moment,
one should again worship those lotuses in the sequence beginning with the *ājñācakra* using their respective syllables, [and then] with the root mantra "so 'ham."
One should place [the breath] in the support at its own station; having meditated upon the supreme goddess Kuṇḍalinī according to the sequence of ascending and descending,
one should perform the prāṇāyāma, the assignment of the ṛṣis and so forth, and the nyāsa of the six limbs.

Having performed the recitation according to one's ability in the sequence to be described hereafter, and having again offered the recitation through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the *mṛṣyā* [mantra], and so forth, as well as the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and so on;

Having thus entrusted her own duties [to him], she thought: "O Mother of the World, whatever I do from morning until evening and from evening back to morning, let that be your worship performed through my own work."
For the sake of performing [this] practice, by the command of your feet alone, O Śrī Sundarī, [I approach] the Lord who consists of the consciousness of the three worlds.

Having risen early in the morning, for the sake of your pleasure, I shall follow the course of worldly existence; O Sovereign Lady of Śrī Tripura, as I follow the course of worldly existence, may rivalry, contempt, strife, and... [by your command].
O Father, do not overcome me with this delusion;
I know not dharma, nor is there any inclination toward it in me, and I know not adharma, nor is there any turning away from it in me— by you, O Hṛṣīkeśa who dwells within my heart.
"I shall act exactly as I have been commanded"—
having thus sought the Queen's command, [he performed] the root-channels (mūlādhāra), svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, and anāhata, which are the foundation of the silent recitation (ajapājapa).
To the deities beginning with Śrī Gaṇapati, who reside from the Viśuddha-āñcakra and Mūlādhāra up to the twelve-angled cakra (dvādaśānta-cakra), [and] to the venerable Guru...

Having offered the innate, spontaneously accomplished *ajapājapa*—which consists of the inhalation and exhalation (*ucchvāsa-niḥśvāsa*) performed throughout the day and night on this very day, numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred—one recites: *oṃ adya pūrvedyur ahorātra-caritam...* [p.
11a] ...niḥśvāsātmakam ṣaṭśatādhika-ekaviṃśati-sahasram...
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the ajapājapa numbering three thousand," one should offer it as follows:
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ [to the Goddess] residing in the mūlādhāra-cakra.
I offer six hundred repetitions of the *ajapā* mantra to the Lord of the *yagaṇa*; obeisance. 4ṃ. To Brahmā, who resides in the *svādhiṣṭhāna* cakra, together with the Śakti Brāhmī.
I offer six thousand recitations of the *japa* and *ajapa*; obeisance. 4ṃ. To Viṣṇu, who resides in the *maṇipūraka* cakra, the sovereign of the three worlds, [and his] Vaiṣṇavī Śakti.

I offer six thousand recitations of the *japa* accompanied by [the deity] residing in the *anāhata-cakra*, together with the *raudra-śakti*; obeisance. 4ṃ. I offer six thousand recitations of the *japa* accompanied by [the deity] residing in the *anāhata-cakra*, together with the *raudra-śakti*.
I offer six thousand [times]; obeisance!
pṛ0 11ba) 4ṃ To the Jīvātman residing in the Viśuddhi-cakra, I offer one thousand recitations; obeisance. 4ṃ To the Paramātman residing in the Ājñā-cakra, [I offer] the recitations...
I offer one thousand [repetitions]; obeisance. 4ṃ.
To the sandals of the venerable Guru situated in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus, I offer one thousand ajapā-japas.
Having offered the recitation of the *ajapā* with "I offer, obeisance," one should perform *prāṇāyāma* with the *ajapā* mantra:
"Oṃ, of this venerable *ajapā-gāyatrī* mantra, Haṃ..."

The sage is [Brahmā], the meter is the unmanifest Gāyatrī, the deity is the Paramahaṃsa, the seed-syllable is *Haṃ*, the power is *Saḥ*, the bolt is *Sohaṃ*, the principle is the syllable *Oṃ*, the vowel accent is Udātta, the color is that of the sky,
and it is employed in my recitation for the sake of liberation.

"Yogaḥ" is for the *añjali* (salutation with joined palms); "Haṃsānena ṛṣaye namaḥ" is for the head; "Avyakta-gāyatrī-cchandasena namaḥ" is for the face; and "Paramahaṃsa-devatāyai" [is for the heart].
*Namaḥ* to the seed-syllable *Haṃ* in the heart; *namaḥ* to the power (*śakti*) *Saḥ* at the *mūlādhāra*; *namaḥ* to the *kīlaka* *So'haṃ* in the feet;
*namaḥ* to the principle (*tattva*) of the syllable *Oṃ* in the heart.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Obeisance to the one of noble voice in the throat; obeisance to the one abiding in the sky in the head; obeisance to the one of golden color in all limbs," [one should contemplate] dharma, artha, and kāma.
One should say with palms joined in reverence for the purpose of the ritual application:
"4ṃ hsāṃ, obeisance to the two thumbs, O you whose essence is the digit of the Sun; 4ṃ hsīṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers, O you whose essence is the Moon."
4ṃ Hsūṃ, svāhā to the self that is stainless collyrium (nirāñjana), with the two middle fingers;
4ṃ Hsaiṃ, svāhā to the self that is without appearance (nirābhāsa), with the two ring fingers; Huṃ, 4ṃ Hsāṃ, [obeisance] to the one whose body is infinite (anantatanu).

May Kṣmādevī impel [this], svāhā! With the little fingers (kaniṣṭhikā), vauṣaṭ! 4ṃ. To the individual soul (jīvātman) residing in the Viśuddhi-cakra, I offer one thousand recitations of the Ajapā-mantra; obeisance! 4ṃ. To the Supreme Soul (paramātman) residing in the Ājñā-cakra, I offer one thousand recitations of the Ajapā-mantra; obeisance!
Having thus offered the recitation of the Ajapā, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the Ajapā mantra:

*Oṃ. Of this Śrī Ajapā Gāyatrī mantra, Haṃ is the Seer (ṛṣi), the unmanifest Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Paramahaṃsa is the deity (devatā), Haṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Saḥ is the power (śakti), So'haṃ is the bolt (kīlaka), Oṃkāra is the essence (tattva), Udātta is the accent (svara), the sky is the location (sthāna), the golden color is the complexion (varṇa); its application (viniyoga) is in my recitation for the sake of liberation.*

Thus is the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*): *Haṃsātmane ṛṣaye namaḥ*—Salutation to the Seer, the Soul of the Swan, on the head. *Avyaktagāyatrīcchandasena namaḥ*—Salutation to the Unmanifest Gāyatrī metre, on the mouth. *Paramahaṃsāya devatāyai namaḥ*—Salutation to the Deity, the Supreme Swan, on the heart. *Haṃ bījāya namaḥ*—Salutation to the Seed-syllable *Haṃ*, at the *mūlādhāra*. *Saḥ śaktaye namaḥ*—Salutation to the Power (*śakti*), on the feet. *So'haṃ kīlakāya namaḥ*—Salutation to the Pin (*kīlaka*), "I am He," on the navel. *Oṃkāratattvāya namaḥ*—Salutation to the Principle of the *Oṃ* syllable, on the heart. *Udāttaḥ svarāya namaḥ*—Salutation to the Acute Accent (*udātta*), on the throat. *Nabhasaḥ sthānāya namaḥ*—Salutation to the Abode of Space, on the crown of the head. *Haimaḥ varṇāya namaḥ*—Salutation to the Golden-colored [syllable].

Having thus assigned [the mantras] to all [the limbs], the application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of *dharma*, *artha*, *kāma*, and *mokṣa*. With palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should say: *Oṃ hsāṃ sūryakalātmane aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ* (4) *Hsīṃ somātmane tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ* (4) *Hsūṃ nirañjanātmane madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ* (4) *Hsaiṃ nirābhāsātmane anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ* (4) *Hsaḥ avyaktabodhātmane svāhā karatalakarapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ phaṭ* Thus is the assignment of the hands (*kara-nyāsa*).

The *ḍga-nyāsa*: Then one should meditate thus: "Oṃ, He whose head the wise declare to be heaven, whose navel is the sky, whose two eyes are the moon and the sun, whose ears are the quarters of space, and whose feet are the earth."
"One should meditate upon Him as the inner self of all beings"—
having thus meditated upon one's own self as having the nature of Virāṭ and contemplating that,
[one should perform] the inhalation and exhalation of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*).
Having recited the *haṃsa* mantra twenty-five times and offered it, one should,
according to the path instructed by the Guru,
preceded by the contemplation of the *nāda*, [proceed with] the performance of all duties free from all superimpositions.

"O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose body is the circle of mountains, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive the touch of my feet. Having thus entreated the Earth, [he should perform] the exhalations...
Having placed his foot upon that [ground] with its essence, reciting the root mantra at every step,
he goes outside the house and traverses a distance of one *śara-kṣepa* (the range of an arrow-shot) toward either the south-west or the southern direction.

Having performed the purification of impure urine and its discharge, as well as the rites of ritual sipping (ācamana), cleaning the teeth, and so forth, on days not prohibited [for such acts], one should, using prescribed wood, [utter] *klīṃ kāmadevāya sarvajana...*
Having cleansed the teeth with the mantra "Obeisance to the beloved one" (*priyāya namaḥ*), discarded the washed tooth-stick in a pure place,
rinsed the mouth with the root-mantra (*mūla*), and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), [he should proceed] to the riverbank.
"One should perform the bath"—this is the rule for the preliminary procedure.
Now follows the ritual for bathing (*snānavidhi*). Therein, first, having washed the water with "Astrāya phaṭ," one should place earth there.
*Pya aim ātmatattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā*. *Klīṃ vidyātattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā*. *Sauḥ śaktitattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā*. Or else:

Having sipped water with *kṣrīṃ svāhā* while recollecting the root mantra, and having performed the bath for the removal of impurities (*malāpakarṣaṇa-snāna*), one should sip water again and stand in water reaching up to the navel, [reciting]: *oṃ adya tāvat tithau*.
On the [specific] lunar day of the [specific] fortnight of the month of [specific] Vadya,
at this time, in this field, I, [name], for the sake of pleasing the venerable Tripurabhairavī, perform this bath according to the Trika ritual.

Having formed the resolve, "I shall offer libations," and having drawn a triangular wheel in the water, [he should invoke: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, and Narmadā, [come] from the solar orb!"
"O Sindhu and Kāverī, please come into this water!

Having thus invoked the sacred waters (tīrtha) with the goad-mudrā (aṅkuśamudrā) and joined them with the previously prepared water, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and sprinkle himself.
Having performed the ritual bathing with clay while reciting the *mūlamantra*,
and having invoked one’s own deity by means of the *kumbhamudrā* while reciting the *mūlamantra*, one should sprinkle [the deity] three times and block the seven apertures, beginning with the ears.
Having submerged oneself three times and emerged, this is the procedure for bathing.

Now, regarding the *saṃdhyā*: there, having sipped water as before, and having performed the *prāṇāyāma* of one’s own root-mantra along with the *ṛṣi*-formula and so forth, as well as the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the hands... [the rest of the text follows].

Having invoked the *tīrtha* residing within oneself and placed that water in the right hand, covering it with the left hand, one should consecrate it seven times with the five elemental mantras: *laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ haṃ*. Then, [reciting] the *mūla*...
Having consecrated the water with the *avidyā* mantra three times, one should sprinkle it seven times upon one's own head with the *tattva-mudrā* formed by the left hand; then,
one should meditate on the remaining water as being of the nature of light (*tejas*).

Having drawn [the impurity] out with the *tvāiḍā* breath, washed away the sin within the body, and having expelled that black-colored water— which is the form of sin— through the *piṅgalā* breath onto the diamond-stone (*vajraśilā*) placed in the left part;
One should cast it with the utterance "phaṭ."
Then, having prepared the *arghya* offering, [one should recite] three times: "Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, to the illustrious Mārtaṇḍabhairava together with the Śakti Prakāśā, I offer this *arghya*, svāhā."

Having offered water for the feet (*arghya*) to the Sun of the *Kula*, and having led the Root Goddess from the heart-lotus into the solar mandala, one should meditate upon her there according to the prescribed rule:
"Oṃ, we know Vāgīśvarī; Klīṃ, Kāmeśvarī, [we meditate upon]..."
"May that power of the buffalo-slayer impel us"—
with this root *gāyatrī*, having offered *arghya* to the Root Goddess within the solar orb during the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*), as follows:

Then, during the four junctions of the day, the practitioner should recite the *śakti* mantra while sequentially drawing forth the splendor of the Goddess from the *mūlādhāra*, the heart-lotus, the space between the eyebrows, and the *brahmarandhra*.
Then, via the *iḍā*...

Having performed the purification by exhaling, having projected [the elements] into the circles of Fire, Sun, and Moon as they have been conceived, and having meditated there upon the Goddess in the form of Consciousness— whether as a child, a youth, or a mature woman— thereafter, *aiṃ hrīṃ*.
"O Goddess Puredevi, we know you; O Kāmeśvarī, we meditate upon you;
may your power impel us. Thus at dawn: "Klīṃ, O Goddess Tripurā, we know you; O Kāmeśvarī, we meditate upon you."
"May that Amṛtā inspire us"—this is for the evening.
"O Vāgīśvarī, we know you; O Kāmēśvarī, may you increase our intellect;
may that Śakti inspire us"—this is for midnight.

Having offered *arghya* with the respective *gāyatrī* mantras for each of the three [deities], having recited their respective *gāyatrīs* according to one's capacity, and having again recited the root *gāyatrī*,
one should perform *prāṇāyāma* along with the *ṛṣi*, etc., and the ritual of the hands (*kara*).
Having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and having recited the root mantra according to one's capacity, and after the recitation, the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*),
and the subsequent six-limbed placement beginning with the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, [he should perform] the "secret" [placement].
Having extracted the splendor of the goddess from the mandalas.

Having brought [the deities] to their respective places and having brought the Goddess into one's own heart, one should meditate upon her there according to the rules and then dismiss the sacred waters (tīrthas).
This is the procedure for the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā-vidhi). Now follows the libation (tarpaṇa). Regarding that:

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) as before, and having performed the breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the assignment of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, and the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should invoke the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and transform the water into nectar seven times with the root mantra using the *amṛtamudrā*.

Having meditated upon the water-machine there, and having brought the Goddess together with her retinue from one's own heart, one should perform the ritual unification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) through the yoga of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*),
and by means of the practice of *kuṇḍalinī*, [the nectar].
Having entered there and worshipped according to the rules, one should satisfy [the deity] three times with the mantra *oṃ śā nyā oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ gurubhairavas tṛpyatām*,
and likewise [satisfy] the supreme guru in the southeast.

"May the Nairṛtya Ravautṛpyatām be satisfied," [recite] four times; "May the Paramācārya Gurubhairava be satisfied," [recite] four times in the Vāyavya; "May the Parameṣṭhiguru be satisfied," [recite] three times, thus performing the satiation with due honor.
"Oṃ! May the Gurus of the Divine Current (divyaugha), the Siddha Current (siddhaugha), and the Human Current (mānavaugha) be satisfied.
Having thus gratified the Gurus, [one should offer] the root mantra into the central drop (bindu) together with the venerable Śrī Kāmeśvara and his retinue...
"May the venerable Śrī Tripurabhairavī, who is the vehicle for the flow of the nectar following the [planetary] days,
be satisfied. Having thus offered libations three times with the root mantra,
[one offers to] the deities of the retinue of the venerable Śrī Tripurabhairavī.

Having satisfied the retinue deities with the mantra "stṛpyata," and having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other rites, one should dismiss the Goddess into one's own heart; thus it is said that one should dismiss her at the sacred fords (tīrthas).
Then, having taken a water-filled pitcher and other items with the root mantra (mūla), and reciting the root mantra while entering the sacrificial hall (yāgageha),
one should worship the deities of the doorway (dvāradevatā) with water and other offerings.
Om, salutation to Dhātrī on the right;
salutation to Vidhātṛ on the left branch (p. 16b); salutation to Gaṅgā on the right branch; salutation to Yamunā on the left branch.
On the left branch: *oṃ dvāraśriyai namaḥ*; above the threshold:
*dehalyai namaḥ*; below: *vāstupuruṣāya namaḥ*;
and in the middle—having thus worshipped the deities of the door on the left side.

Having entered the interior of the pavilion by contracting [the body] with the left foot leading the way, and having spread a seat there, one should say: *Oṃ hrīṃ ādhāraśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*. Thus...
Having worshipped [the deities] and sat there in the Vīrāsana or other posture, one should perform the purification of the seat (*āsanashodhana*). *Oṃ*,
for this mantra of the purification of the seat, Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*) and Sutala is the meter (*chanda*).
The Kūrma deity is employed for the placement of the seat.
With palms joined in *añjali*, [one says]: "Salutation to Maṇḍūka;
salutation to Kālāgnirudra; salutation to Mūlaprakṛti."
Having worshipped the seat with: "Oṃ Ādhāraśakti, obeisance! Oṃ Kūrma, obeisance! Oṃ Ananta, obeisance! Oṃ Pṛthivī, obeisance! Oṃ Ratnavedikā, obeisance!", [one recites]: "Prīṃ! O Earth, by you..."
"O Goddess who holds the light, you were held by Viṣṇu; O Goddess, hold me and make this seat pure. Having thus addressed the Earth, one should accept the *saṃvid* according to the mantra.

The procedure for that is as follows: Oṃ, O Consciousness, born of Brahman, daughter of Brahman, ever sinless; for the sake of the satisfaction of the Brāhmaṇas, be pure at all times. Oṃ, obeisance to Brāhmāṇī, svāhā.

Oṃ, O Goddess who destroys the root of obstacles, who awakens deficient understanding, who brings kings and subjects under control, and who slays the faction of enemies! Oṃ, obeisance to the Kṣatriya woman, svāhā! Oṃ!
O fire whose flames are kindled by the fuel of ignorance, O fire of knowledge whose form is Brahman, grant me the oblation of bliss, joy, and perfect knowledge.
*Hrīṃ*, obeisance to Vaiśyā, Svāhā! I bow down; obeisance!
O Mother who bestows the path of the yoga of samādhi, conqueror of the three worlds,
[grant] the fruit of samādhi!
*dābhava klīṃ śūdrāyai namaḥ svāhā*— with this mantra;
*oṃ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtam ākarṣaya 2 siddhiṃ dehi śrītripura*.

"Bhairavī-padaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā. Having consecrated [the object] with this mantra, [one says]: "Come, come! Stay, stay! Be present, be present! Be firmly established, be firmly established! Be present, be present! Be present, be present! Be present, be present! Above that, [recite] the mūla..."
Having recited "Laṃ" seven times, having rendered [the substance] nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*,
having displayed the mudrās for invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, and having performed the binding of the ten directions with the *koṭika* [mudrās], [he should place it] upon his own head.
Having gratified [the deity] and having fully satisfied the root goddess within one's own heart (pṛ.
18a), [one recites]: *oṃ aiṃ vada vada vāgvādini mama jihvāgre sthirībhava sarvasattvavaśaṅkari svāhā*. Thus...
One should offer oblations into the mouth; then, having become composed of bliss, [one recites]:
"Oṃ, may those beings depart who are situated upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish."
"By the command of Śiva, may those who cause heresy— whether they be living beings or non-beings,
whether dwelling on earth, in the intermediate space, or in the divine worlds—
be destroyed by this [mantra] through the command of Śiva. Thus ends the *tarjanī* (threatening gesture).

Having dispelled the three types of obstacles with divine vision by raising the two middle fingers three times upward and striking the left heel three times, [he should perform] ten snaps of the fingers.
Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and visualized a rampart of fire in the four directions, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) as follows:
there, reciting the *praṇava* sixteen times while [holding] the right thumb...

Having blocked the right nostril with the thumb, one should fill [the lungs] with air through the left; then, having released that same [air], one should block the left nostril with the ring finger and the little finger [of the right hand] and exhale it sixty-four times.
Having restrained the breath with both [nostrils], one should perform kumbhaka;
then, while reciting that same [mantra] thirty-two times, one should likewise restrain the breath through the left nostril and exhale it through the right.
This is one breath-control (prāṇāyāma); by the reverse order, this is the second; and the first is the third. In this way, one's entire body, though defiled, becomes fit for the worship of the deity.

One should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) as follows: having brought Kuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra along with the Earth element by means of the mantra "Haṃ Saḥ," one should bring her to the Svādhiṣṭhāna, and there, into the water...
Having meditated on [the water] dissolved into the earth, one should bring it back into the jewel-vessel along with that water;
having meditated there upon the water dissolved into fire, one should [bring it] back into the *ānāha* (the navel center) along with that fire.
Having meditated upon the fire as dissolved there in the wind, one should draw it out together with the wind;
having purified it and brought it back, one should meditate upon that wind as dissolved there in the ether. From that ether...
Having brought [the breath] into the *ājñā-cakra* along with the vital energy (*śena*), one should contemplate the space situated there as dissolved therein; having perceived the mind as dissolved,
and having entrusted the traveler to the path of the wayfarer, [one should focus on] the thousand-petaled lotus.

Having offered that supreme Śivā, who exists in the form of a radiant bindu within the triangle situated in the center of the lunar disc located at the root of the ear, according to the procedure for breath control (prāṇāyāma),...
One should meditate on the seed-syllable of air (*miti*), smoke-colored; by reciting it sixteen times, one should visualize the personified sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) situated in the left side of the body—
a personified sin with the luster of collyrium, [the size of] a Brahmin-killer...
And [the rule] is without that head.
The two arms represent the theft of gold; the heart is joined with the drinking of liquor;

the two hips represent violating the Guru’s bed; the two feet represent association with such persons; minor limbs represent the minor sins (upapātaka); and the entire body represents the mortal sins (mahāpātaka).

One should visualize a wicked, angry being with red beard and eyes, holding a sword and a shield, within the belly; having thus visualized him, one should dry him up by means of the fire-seed syllable *raṃ* four times.
Reciting that same [mantra] sixty times while burning it, one should contemplate the seed-syllable *amṛta* (the syllable of immortality), white in color, within the thousand-spoked [wheel];
then, reciting it thirty-two times, by means of the rain of nectar arising from that, [one should perform the rite].
Having produced a body free from sin and having made it very firm by means of the yellow-colored *pṛthvī* seed-syllable at the surface of the forehead,
[one should worship] with the mantra *hrīṃ*, which is Bhuvaneśvarī, together with her consort.
Having performed this [rite], by means of the mantra *so'ham*, he [the practitioner] places the five elements— which have become as if longing for nectar—
and the individual soul (*jīvātman*) into their respective locations via the path of Brahman (*brahmapatha*).
One should thus perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Then, having contemplated oneself in the form of the deity and placed the hand upon the heart, one should perform the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) as follows: Oṃ...
Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ haṃsaḥ. Oṃ, the vital breaths (prāṇas) of the illustrious Tripurabhairavī are here;
13ṃ, the life-force (jīva) is established here; 13ṃ, all the sense organs (sarvendriyāṇi) are established here; 13ṃ, speech and mind...
Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) with the mantra: "O eye, ear, nose,
and life-breath, come here, O auspicious one, stay here for a long time, svāhā," one should perform the recollection of one's own *mūla-mantra* and so forth.
Om. Of this mantra of the venerable Śrī Tripurabhairavī, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandaḥ),
the venerable Tripurabhairavī is the deity (devatā), hsraiṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), and hsrauṃ is the power (śakti).
The power (*śakti*) is *hsrīṃ*; the pivot (*kīlaka*) is "for me, for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation"; the application (*viniyoga*) is in the recitation (*japa*).
Having thus remembered with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the rules.
Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the Ṛṣi—on the head. Salutation to Paṅkti, the metre—on the mouth. Salutation to Śrī Tripurabhairavī, the deity—on the heart. Hsraiṃ.
*Vījāya namaḥ* at the secret place; *hsrauṃ śaktaye namaḥ* at the feet; *hasklīṃ kīlakāya namaḥ* at the navel;
[this is] for the purpose of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and for application during recitation (*japa*).
"Yoga" refers to [the placement] on all limbs. Thus is the recollection of the seer and so forth:
*hsraiṃ namaḥ* from the navel to the feet; *hstrīṃ namaḥ* from the throat to the navel; *hsrauṃ namaḥ* [from the head to the throat].
From the crown of the head to the throat: *hsraiṃ namaḥ*. On the sole of the left foot: *hsrīṃ namaḥ*; on the right: *hsrauṃ namaḥ*; on both: *drāṃ kṣobhaṇabāṇāya namaḥ* (on the thumbs);
*drīṃ drāvaṇabāṇāya namaḥ* (on the index fingers);
*klīṃ ākarṣaṇabāṇāya namaḥ* (on the middle fingers).
*Ṛṣaṇabālāya namaḥ* on the middle fingers; *mluṃ vaśīkaraṇabāṇāya namaḥ* on the ring fingers; *saḥ unmādabāṇāya namaḥ* on the little fingers. Thus.
The placement of the arrows (bāṇanyāsa) is as follows: *sauṃ kāmāya namaḥ* on the two thumbs;
*klīṃ manmathāya namaḥ* on the two index fingers; *aiṃ kandarpāya namaḥ* on the two middle fingers; *nlūṃ makaradhvajāya namaḥ* [on the two ring fingers].
*Anāmayoḥ strīmīnaketavenamaḥ kaniṣṭhayoḥ*. Thus is the *kāma-nyāsa*. Now follows the *svamūla-kara-nyāsa*:
*Hsrāṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *Hsklhrīṃ tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ*.
Svāhā to the two thumbs, Hsrūṃ to the two middle fingers, Vaṣaṭ to the two ring fingers, Huṃ to the two little fingers,
Vauṣaṭ to the two palms and backs of the hands, Phaṭ to Hsraṃḥ.

Now, the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): *hsrāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hsrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *hsrūṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *hsraiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *hsraiṃ* [to the eyes, *vauṣaṭ*].
*Netratrayāya* auṣaṭ; *Hsrāṃ* *astrāya* phaṭ.
Now, the Mātṛkā-nyāsa: for this venerable Antamātṛkā-nyāsa, Brahmā is the Ṛṣi and Gāyatrī is the metre.
The meter is Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī; the deity is Haḥ; the seed-syllables are Loṃ; the powers are the vowels; the unmanifest is the bolt;
[this is] the Nyāsa as a limb of mine, Śrī Tripurabhairavī.
Having remembered the *sevini-yoga* with palms joined in reverence (*prāñjali*), one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*):
"Salutation to Brahmā-Ṛṣi" on the head; "Salutation to Gāyatrī-chandas" on the mouth; [and] "Salutation to Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī-devatā."

Salutation to *tāyainamaḥ* in the heart; salutation to the seed-syllables (*vīja*) for the *hal* letters in the secret place; salutation to the vowels (*svara*) as the powers (*śakti*) in the feet; salutation to the unmanifest pillar (*avyaktakīlaka*) in the navel; [and salutation] to my Śrītri...
The application [of mantras] as limbs for the worship of Purabhairavī is as follows:
(p. 22a) The *nyāsa* on all limbs and hands: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ kaṃ 5ṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ hṛdayāya* (to the heart), *4ṃ iṃ caṃ 5ṃ*.
*Īṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā* to the head; *uṃ ṛṃ* *ūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock; *eṃ taṃ* *aiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *huṃ* to the armor; *oṃ paṃ* *5ṃ*.
*Oṃ* to the thumbs and little fingers, *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes;
*aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ* to the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*).
Thus, [the mudrās] are performed from the thumbs to the palms of the two hands.
One should likewise assign these same mantras to the six limbs, beginning with the heart;
thereafter, one should assign the internal Mātṛkā:
*aṃ naṃ* [to the heart], *āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ* [to the head].
Aṃ Āṃ at the throat in the sixteen-petaled [lotus]: Kaṃ Namaḥ, Khaṃ Gaṃ Ghaṃ Ṅaṃ Caṃ Chaṃ Jaṃ Jhaṃ Ñaṃ, Ṭaṃ Ṭhaṃ Namaḥ; in the twelve-petaled [lotus] at the anāhata [cakra].

*Ḍaṃ namaḥ*, *ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ namaḥ* at the navel on the ten-petalled lotus; *yaṃ namaḥ*, *baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ* at the base of the liṅga on the six-petalled lotus; *śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ namaḥ* at the *mūlādhāra* on the four-petalled lotus; *haṃ namaḥ*, *kṣaṃ namaḥ* between the eyebrows.
This is the internal Mātṛkā-nyāsa on the two petals; alternatively, there is the external Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
In that regard, the ṛṣi and other [limbs] are as in the internal Mātṛkā, but the placement (nyāsa) is as follows:
*4ṃ aṃ namaḥ śirasi*.
4ṃ Āṃ on the face; 4ṃ Iṃ on the right eye; 4ṃ Īṃ on the left; 4ṃ Uṃ on the right ear; 4ṃ Ūṃ on the left; 4ṃ Ṛṃ on the right nostril; 4ṃ Ṝṃ on the left; 4ṃ Ḷṃ on the right cheek; 4ṃ Ḹṃ on the left.
Eṃ on the upper lip; 4ṃ aiṃ on the lower lip; 4ṃ oṃ on the upper teeth; 4ṃ auṃ on the lower teeth;
4ṃ aṃ on the head; 4ṃ aḥ on the mouth; 4ṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ on the joints and tips of the right arm; 4ṃ caṃ chaṃ... [and so forth].

Jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ at the joints and tips of the left arm; 4ṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ at the joints and tips of the right foot; 4ṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ at the joints and tips of the left foot; 4ṃ paṃ on the right side; 4ṃ phaṃ.
On the left [shoulder] 4ṃ baṃ; on the back 4ṃ bhaṃ; at the navel 4ṃ maṃ;
in the abdomen 4ṃ yaṃ—*namaḥ* to the skin-self; in the heart 4ṃ raṃ—*namaḥ* to the blood-self;
on the right shoulder 4ṃ laṃ—*namaḥ* to the flesh-self; on the hump [of the spine].

4ṃ Vaṃ, obeisance to the self consisting of fat; on the left shoulder. 4ṃ Śaṃ, obeisance to the self consisting of bone; from the heart to the end of the right hand. 4ṃ Ṣaṃ, obeisance to the self consisting of marrow; from the heart to the end of the left hand. 4ṃ Saṃ, [obeisance to] the self consisting of semen...
4ṃ Haṃ: Salutation to the Prāṇātman from the heart to the right foot. 4ṃ Laṃ: Salutation to the Jīvātman from the feet to the heart. 4ṃ Kṣaḥ.
From the heart to the top of the head of the Supreme Self— thus is the external Mātṛkā-nyāsa. [One should meditate on her] whose form consists of the fifty letters,
who is adorned by the crescent moon, and who resembles pure crystal.
resplendent with a garment of fine silk.
(Page 23b) Bearing a rosary, a water-pot, a book, and the gesture of granting boons, and adorned with ornaments shimmering with pearls and gems—
thus is the placement of the Mother (Mātṛkā-nyāsa). Now, the placement of the Vidyā (Vidyā-nyāsa)...
He [should place]: *hsraiṃ namaḥ* on the neck-jewel (*maṇikaṇṭha*), *hsklhrīṃ namaḥ* on the palm, and *hsrauṃ namaḥ* on the tip;
likewise on the right hand, he places *hsraiṃ namaḥ* on the wrist (*kakṣyā*) and *hsklhrīṃ namaḥ* on the elbow (*kurpa*).
Hsrauṃ Namaḥ on the right hand; likewise on the left, Vā Hauca Hsraiṃ Namaḥ on the girdle of the feet; Hsklhrīṃ Namaḥ on the knees;
Hsrauṃ Namaḥ on the tips of the feet; likewise on the left.
*Hsraiṃ namaḥ* on the feet; *Hsklhrīṃ namaḥ* on the genitals; *Hasrāṃ namaḥ* on the heart; and at the end of the feet—this is the *vidyā-nyāsa*.
Now, the *navayoni-nyāsa*: *Hsraiṃ namaḥ* on the right [shoulder].

*Hs-k-l-hr-īṃ namaḥ* on the left [ear]; *Hs-rauṃ namaḥ* on the chin (1); *Hs-raiṃ namaḥ* on the right temple; *Hs-k-l-hr-īṃ namaḥ* on the left [temple] (p. 24a); *Hs-rauṃ namaḥ* on the mouth (2); *Hs-raiṃ namaḥ* on the right eye.

*Hsklhrīṃ namaḥ* on the left; *hsrauṃ namaḥ* on the nose; 3. *hasraiṃ namaḥ* on the right arm; *hslhrīṃ namaḥ* on the left; *hsrauṃ namaḥ* on the heart; 4. *hasraiṃ namaḥ* on the right elbow; *hsklhrīṃ namaḥ*.

On the left [shoulder], *hsrauṃ namaḥ* at the belly; 5. *hsraiṃ namaḥ* on the right knee; *hsklīṃ namaḥ* on the left [knee]; *hsrauṃ namaḥ* at the navel; 6. *hsraiṃ namaḥ* on the right foot; *hsklhrīṃ namaḥ* on the left [foot]; *hsrauṃ namaḥ*.
At the secret place (guhya): *hsraiṃ namaḥ*; on the right side (*dakṣapārśve*): *hsklhrīṃ namaḥ*;

on the left (*vāme*): *hsrauṃ namaḥ*; at the heart (*hṛdi*): *8 hsraiṃ*; on the right breast (*dakṣastane*): *hsklhrīṃ namaḥ*; on the left (*vāme*): *hsrauṃ namaḥ*; at the throat (*kaṇṭhe*): *9*. Thus it is said.
The placement of the vital breaths.
pṛ0 24ba) Then again, according to the oral tradition (saṃpradāya), the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa):
hsraiṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ 3; hsklhrīṃ śirase svāhā 2; hsrauṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ 3; hsrauṃ...
*Hūṃ* for the armor; *Hsklhrīṃ* *vauṣaṭ* for the three eyes;
*Hsrauṃ* *phaṭ* twice for the weapon—by these *nyāsa*s, having purified the body, one should meditate on the Root Mantra at the *mūlādhāra* as being like ten million flashes of lightning.

O Beloved, that [power] has an equal radiance, resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons; its nature is like a lotus fiber, and it possesses three folds, O slender one— this is the upward-moving power (ūrdhvaśakti).
O fair-faced one, by means of the innate *pāta* [descent] through the firmness of the root power (*mūla-śakti*),
the central power (*madhya-śakti*) is awakened; one should contemplate the supreme bliss, the mass of ultimate joy— thus ends [the section].
Having performed the ritual fanning, one should worship the seat (*pīṭha*) within one's own body by means of placement (*nyāsa*).
At the *mūlādhāra*: "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti; obeisance to Prakṛti; obeisance to Kamaṭha; obeisance to Śeṣa. [Page 25a] Obeisance to Pṛthivī.
Salutation to the Earth; salutation to the excellent nectar; salutation to the jeweled island;
salutation to the wish-fulfilling gem palace; salutation to the jeweled altar; salutation to the jeweled pedestal; salutation to the lamp...
Salutation to the various hosts of sages; salutation to the various gods;
salutation to Dharma on the left thigh; salutation to Aiśvarya on the right thigh;
salutation to Adharma on the face.

Salutation to Ajñāna (Ignorance) on the right back; salutation to Avairāgya (Non-detachment) on the left back; salutation to Anaiśvarya (Lack of sovereignty) at the heart; salutation to Śeṣa; salutation to Padma; salutation to Prakṛti.
Salutation to the petals consisting of illusion; salutation to the filaments consisting of transformation; salutation to the pericarp adorned with the fifty letters;
salutation to the solar disc; salutation to the lunar [disc].
Homage to the Maṇḍalāya.
Oṃ, salutation to Vaiśvānara-maṇḍala; salutation to Saṃsatva; salutation to Raṃ Rajas; salutation to Taṃ Tamas; salutation to Āṃ Ātman;
salutation to Aṃ Antarātman; salutation to Paṃ Paramātman.
*Namaḥ* to *hrīṃ*, the essence of knowledge; *namaḥ* to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*);
on the petals: *namaḥ* to Vāmā, *namaḥ* to Jyeṣṭhā, *namaḥ* to Raudrī, *namaḥ* to Ambikā, [and] *namaḥ* to Icchā.
Salutations to Jñānā; salutations to Kriyā;
salutations to Kubjikā; salutations to Citrā; salutations to Viṣaghnīkā; salutations to Dūtī.
Oṃ, obeisance to Ānandā; in the center, obeisance to Mano-manī;
Aiṃ, obeisance to Parā; obeisance to Aparā; obeisance to Parāparā;
Hsauṃḥ, obeisance to Sadāśiva, the Great Preta.
Salutation to the lotus posture; salutation to the couch of Supreme Śiva;
salutation to that which is variegated and adorned with the brilliance of the jewels in the crown, and [to that] which possesses a garland of heads dripping with blood, fat, and phlegm.
(Aligned with the text on p. 26a) She who possesses the beauty of three eyes, endowed with a face like the full moon, whose full, high, and firm breasts shine with strings of pearl necklaces,
marked by the three folds of her waist, and adorned with various ornaments.

Adorned, clothed in red garments, intoxicated by youth, and possessing a beautiful form; holding a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary and the gesture of granting boons in her right hands— she is the eternal one, the great prosperity.

One should remember [the mantra] "pradāṃsmaret"; having thus meditated upon the auspicious Bhairavī Tripurā and worshipped her with mental offerings (mānasopacāra), one should perform mentally, according to one's capacity, the recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and so forth, [visualizing] the Kāmakalā.

Having contemplated that, one should meditate upon the venerable Tripurā-Bhairavī as described above, and while doing so, one should prepare the general *arghya* on one's left; on the ground to one's right, one should fashion a circular mandala consisting of a triangle.
Having worshipped the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) there and placed the support (ādhāra) upon it, [one should place] the vessel purified with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) on top of that.
Having placed a vessel, such as a conch or the like, filled with water while reciting the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*),
one should invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) there, beginning with "O Gaṅgā," and having offered perfumes (*gandha*) and other substances while reciting the *praṇava* (OM),
[one should worship] Fire, Sun, and...
Having worshipped with all [the offerings] and displayed the *dhenumudrā*,
one should worship with one's own mantra; this is the procedure for the general *arghya* water as prescribed by rule, and then [one should offer it] from one's own vessel.
Having prepared a maṇḍala consisting of two triangles situated within a six-cornered hexagon, with a square outside the points [of the triangles],
and having sprinkled it with the water of the general *arghya*, one should place the support there.

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings according to the sequence of the pedestal worship (*pīṭhapūjā*) beginning with "Obeisance to Ra-śakti," one should wash the support (*ādhāra*) with *namaḥ*, place it upon the mandala, and [proceed with] *raṃ va*.

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to the one whose self is the ten digits of the lunar orb," and having rinsed the water-pot (kalaśa) with "Phaṭ," filled it with water, and adorned it with red cloth, garlands, and so forth; [page 27a]... [it is] fully prepared.
Having established [the deity] there with the thought of it being the support for the lamentation,
one should worship the jar with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the sun-maṇḍala consisting of twelve kalās," and then [worship] "Oṃ, to the moon-maṇḍala consisting of sixteen..."
Having worshipped the substance with "śakalātmane namas," having protected it with "phaṭ," having veiled it with "hūm," having gazed upon it with the root mantra,
having sprinkled it with "namaḥ," and having smelled the fragrance with the root mantra, [one should place] the *kuṇḍa*...
Having offered a *bhepuṣpa* flower, one should perform the rite for release from the curse:
"O Supreme Brahman, who are eternally composed of both the gross and the subtle—where could the sin of killing a Brahmin possibly arise? By that [truth], may I be purified."
O you who are born from the solar disc, born from the abode of Varuṇa,
consisting of the seed-syllable *am*,
be liberated from the curse of Śukra.
Let it be cast off.

"O Goddess, if the *praṇava* is the seed of the Vedas and consists of the bliss of Brahman, by that truth may the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) be removed. (Recite this) three times. *Oṃ vāṃ vīṃ vūṃ vaiṃ vauṃ vaḥ* [removal of] the curse of Brahmā.
"Salutation to the goddess Asurā who has been liberated"—thus also three times.
"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Krāṃ Krīṃ Kraṃ Kraiṃ Krauṃ Kraḥ, O Svarā-Kṛṣṇa, release the curse, release it! Cause nectar to flow, cause it to flow! Svāhā! Thus.
Oṃ. The Swan dwelling in the pure, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling at the altar,
the guest dwelling in the house, the dweller in the waters, the dweller in the rays of light, the dweller in truth, the dweller in the sky, born of the waters, born of the rays, born of truth.
Having recited "jādrijāṛtam" three times,
and having meditated there upon Ānandabhairava and Surādevī,
[one should offer] "hasarakṣamalavayūṃ ānandabhairavāya vauṣaṭ."

Having worshipped the God and Goddess three times with the mantra *ṣaṭ saha-kṣa-ma-la-va-ra-yūṃ surā-devyai vauṣaṭ*, [one should place] *aṃ* (16), *kaṃ* (19), and *thaṃ* (16) in three rows moving clockwise in the center of the substances.

Having thus drawn the wheel of powers (śakticakra) and having written the syllables *haṃ* and *kṣaṃ* in its center, one should contemplate nectar within the substance through their immersion, and then transform it into nectar by means of the *vam* syllable and the cow-seal (dhenumudrā).
Having held the vessel while reciting the seed-syllable *Vam*, the nectar-seed,
as well as the root-mantra eight times, and having drawn a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square between oneself and the Śrīcakra;
Salutation to the seat of Turaśrepaṇagiri; salutation to the seat of Uḍḍiyāna; salutation to the seat of Kāmarūpa;
salutation to the seat of Jālandhara—having thus worshipped these six.

Having worshipped the six limbs in the corners, and having worshipped the three sections at the front and right of the triangle with the *trikhaṇḍa* mantra, and having worshipped the foundational powers (*ādhāraśakti*) in the center,
one should install the triple yantra within the interior of the triangle.

Having sprinkled [the area] with water common to all [mantras] while reciting *namaḥ*, [one should worship]: *yaṃ* to Dhūmrārciṣī, *raṃ* to Ūṣmā, *laṃ* to Jvalinī, *vaṃ* to Jvālinī, *śaṃ* to Visphuliṅginī, and *ṣaṃ* to Suśrī.

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Saṃsvarūpā, Haṃ Kapilā, Laṃ Havyavāhā, and Kṣaḥ Kavyavāhā," one should worship in the center [the syllable] Raṃ with "Obeisance to the Fire-maṇḍala consisting of ten kalās."
Having honored [the vessel] with "Maḥ," having worshipped the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in the six corners,
and having worshipped the Goddess in the center with the root mantra (mūla), one should wash the vessel with "Phaṭ" and place it upon the tripod (yaṃtrikā).

Therein: *kaṃ* *khaṃ* obeisance to Tāpinī; *gaṃ* *ghaṃ* obeisance to Dhūmrā; *ṅaṃ* *caṃ* obeisance to Marīcī; *chaṃ* *jaṃ* obeisance to Jvālinī; *jhaṃ* *ñaṃ* obeisance to Rucī; *ṭaṃ* *ṭhaṃ* obeisance to Su... [and so forth].
Ṣumṇāyai namaḥ; Jaṃthaṃ bhogadāyai namaḥ; Jhaṃ Taṃ viśvāyai namaḥ; Ñaṃ Ṇaṃ bodhinyai namaḥ; Ṭaṃ Iṃ kṣamāyai namaḥ—thus [the seed-syllables] in the center for the solar maṇḍala (arka-maṇḍala).
Having worshipped with [the mantra] "consisting of twelve kalās" (pṛ0 29a), one should draw a triangle, a circle, and a hexagon within the vessel,
worship it with the entire mantra as well as its individual parts, and [worship] Varuṇa.

Reciting the seed-syllable, the root-mantra, and the *mātṛkā* in reverse order, one should fill a triangle with nectar and a hexagon with water; having placed fragrant substances and so forth therein, [one should worship] "Aṃ, to Amṛtā."
Salutation to Āṃ, the giver of honor; salutation to Iṃ, the eastern one; salutation to Īṃ, contentment;
salutation to Uṃ, nourishment; salutation to Ūṃ, delight; salutation to Ṛṃ, fortitude;
salutation to Ṝṃ, Śaśinī; salutation to Ḷṃ, and...
Oṃ *dṛgāyai* namaḥ; *lṛṃ kāntyai* namaḥ; *eṃ jyotsnāyai* namaḥ; *aiṃ śriyai* namaḥ; *oṃ prītyai* namaḥ;
*auṃ aṅgadāyai* namaḥ; *aṃ pūrṇāyai* namaḥ.
Having worshipped with "Aḥ pūrṇāmṛtāyai namaḥ" and "Oṃ ṣoḍaśakalātmane somamaṇḍalāya namaḥ," and having written the mantra and the substance as before, [one draws] a triangle.

Having written "aṃ 16 kaṃ 16 thaṃ 16" in three rows upon the three lines, and having worshipped the triangle with the three root-syllables and the six limbs in the six corners, [one should worship] with "Gaṅge... and so forth.

Having invoked the secondary *tīrtha*, and having worshipped [it] starting from the east with the mantra *glūṃ gaganaratnebhyaḥ namaḥ* for Ānandabhairava and the mantra *slūṃ svargaratnebhyaḥ* for Svarādi-vyomva, [one should proceed].

Having worshipped with "Homage to the jewels of the netherworld (pātāla), Plūṃ! Homage to the jewels of the mortal world (martya), Mlūṃ! In the center, homage to the jewels of the serpent-world (nāga), Nlūṃ!", one should purify the second and subsequent [levels].
Having veiled [the deity] with *hūṃ* and rendered it nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛtya*), having bound the directions with three *tāla*-claps,
having recited the root mantra seven times over that, having invoked the Goddess there, and having again bound the directions with three *tāla*-claps—
Having veiled [the vessel] with the *nṛtya* mantra, having rendered it nectar (*amṛtīkṛtya*),

having displayed the *yoni-mudrā*, having worshipped with "hsauḥ namaḥ," having displayed the *śaṅkha-mudrā*, and having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkṛtya*) by means of the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*).
Having placed the vessel with the *tasya-mudrā* and recited the root mantra ten times, one should visualize the vessel as the Goddess; then,
having obtained the permission of the Goddess, [one places] the Guru’s vessel near the jar.

Then, having set out the vessel for the *śakti*, the vessel for enjoyment (*bhoga-pātra*), one’s own vessel, the vessel for the *yoginīs*, the vessel for the heroes (*vīra-pātra*), and the vessels for the *bali* offering, the water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), [one performs] the chewing (*carvaṇa*).

Having drawn [the substance] from the *śrīpātra* with the *tattvamudrā* by means of the *yutaka*, one should satisfy Ānandabhairava three times with that mantra: "I satisfy Ānandabhairava; obeisance. Then, the venerable...
"Obeisance; I satiate the feet of the venerable Guru Śrī Kaulānandanātha. Having thus satiated him three times, one should likewise satiate the Paramaguru, the Paramācārya, and the others.

With the nectar from the Śrīpātra, using the root mantra, one should satisfy the venerable Tripurabhairavī—along with her weapons, her vehicle, and her retinue—with the words: "I satisfy [her]; obeisance. Thus concludes the worship of the Kalaśa.

Now, according to the ritual procedure, having placed the Śrīcakra upon the pedestal (pīṭha) and performed the worship of the pedestal as before, one should meditate upon the venerable Tripurabhairavī and [expel the breath] through the left nostril by means of the seed-syllable of air (Yam).
Having brought a handful of flowers from one's own heart and invoked the Goddess there,
[one should recite]: "O Mistress of the Gods, easily attained through devotion, accompanied by your retinue, until I have worshipped you..."
Having recited "Tāvad devī ihāvaha," at the end of the root mantra, one says:
"O Śrī Tripurabhairavī, accompanied by Śrī Kāmeśvara Śiva, come here, come here; stay here, stay here; be present here."

"Hi 2, come here and be established; 2, accept my worship accompanied by all ritual offerings. Having thus displayed the mudrās for invocation and so forth, [perform] the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* over the *śrīcakra*.
Having performed the binding of the ten directions (*daśadigbandha*) with the *liḷihāna* mudrā,
having performed the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), the sakalīkaraṇa, and the paramīkaraṇa, and having displayed the *dhenu*, *yoni*, *vara*, *abhaya*, *pustaka*, and *akṣamālā* [mudrās]...

Having displayed the mudrās of the goad, noose, bow, arrow, skull-cup, lotus, and so forth, [one should worship] her together with her weapons, vehicles, and retinue by means of the nectar from the Śrīpātra.
"Oṃ, I satiate Śrī Tripurabhairavī together with Varaṇā and Śrī Kāmeśvara Bhairava; namaḥ. Having thus satiated her three times, [one should again [satiate] Śrī Tripurabhairavī with the root mantra.]
"Oṃ śrīpādukāṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ"—having thus offered libations three times, and having uttered the root mantra:
"This pādya is offered to Śrī Tripurabhairavī together with Śrī Kāmeśvara; namaḥ."
Water for the feet (pādya) for the two feet; likewise, the respectful offering (arghya) with "svāhā" for the head;
water for sipping (ācamanīya) and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) for the mouth.
Having bathed [the deity] with "snānīyaṃ namaḥ sarvāṅge" (bath-water, salutation to all limbs),
and having sprinkled the body with a clean silk cloth (*śuddhadugūla*), [one should adorn it] with a variegated silken garment,
saffron, musk, sandalwood, vermilion, a crown, and earrings.

Having offered various ornaments such as the three types of necklaces and so forth, one should again offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). Then, with the tips of the middle and index fingers, one should offer scented paste (*gandha*) while reciting "Gandho namaḥ," using the thumb and index finger.
Having worshipped with flowers while reciting "bhyāṃ puṣpāṇi vauṣaṭ," and having worshipped the incense vessel with "dhūpapātraṃ phaṭ" and placed it before [the deity],
one should touch the *śrīpātra* nectar with the left ring finger.
Having offered the incense with the words, "I offer this incense," and having worshipped the bell with the mantra "Oṃ jagaddhuni mantramātaḥ svāhā," he should ring it with his left hand,
using the middle and ring fingers.
Having held the incense with the *guṣṭha* [finger] and reciting the *Gāyatrī* and the root mantra:
"Born from the essence of the forest trees (*vanaspati*), rich in fragrance, the best of scents,
worthy of being smelled by all the gods— may this incense be accepted."
Having offered incense to the goddess who is equal in the three ways with the mantra *hyatāmiti*,
one should then place the lamp in front [of her] and perform worship as before;
having performed the worship, [one should hold] the lamp-vessel with the left middle finger.

Touching the lamp while reciting "I offer the lamp," and having thus offered it as before while ringing the bell, one should hold the middle of the lamp-vessel with the middle finger and thumb and show it while reciting the Gāyatrī.
"Reciting the *Mūla-mantra*, [one should offer] this great lamp, which is clearly radiant, dispelling darkness everywhere, the light both external and internal;
may this lamp be accepted. Thus one should light the lamp.

Then, having prepared a vessel of gold or other material, one should fashion a nine-petaled lotus of saffron in the shape of the moon and place *caru* within it; having established a single lamp in the center and eight lamps upon the eight petals, [one recites] *śrīṃ sauḥ*.
Having worshipped with "glūṃ slūṃ mlūṃ plūṃ nlūṃ soḥ śrīratneśvaryai namaḥ" and having worshipped with the root mantra,
one should lift the vessel up to the top of the head nine times at the end of the root mantra.

"O Goddess, who consists of nine aspects and is joined with the Lord of the Wheel of the Head, accept this *ārātrika* for my attainment. Having said this, one should perform the *nīrājana* with the wheel-mudrā (*cakramudrā*). Then...

Having placed various food offerings (*naivedya*) in a vessel made of gold or other materials, one should veil them with the syllable *huṃ*, transform them into nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*,
and recite the root mantra seven times while holding the offering vessel with the thumb of the left hand.

Touching the divine, excellently prepared supreme food contained in golden vessels, which possesses five types of textures and is endowed with six flavors, [say]: "O Supreme Goddess, accept this; I offer it as a food offering (naivedya)."

One should release [the offering] with the right thumb and forefinger; then, having again offered water for sipping (ācamanīya), one should first present the betel leaf prepared with camphor and other ingredients, saying: "I offer this at the end of the root mantra."
The dismissal of all [the deities] should be performed with the water from the arghya vessel (p.
33a). Then, having thrice gratified the Goddess with the tattva-mudrā and having displayed the previously mentioned mudrās, one should place the yoni-mudrā at the heart.
Having displayed the five mudrās— Kṣobhaṇī at the mouth, Drāviṇī between the eyebrows, Ākarṣiṇī on the forehead, Vaśinī in the Brahma-randhra, and Hlādinī— she was thus made manifest.
With palms joined in *añjali*, having received the command by saying, "O Goddess of Devas, Śrī Tripurabhairavī, I worship the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*)," one should begin the worship of the enclosure.
Therein, first, at the eastern *yoni*:
In the space between the two middle *yoni*s, at the end of the Guru-mantra:
I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the venerable Śrī Kolānandanātha; obeisance! I offer libations; obeisance! Supreme!
One should worship and offer libations to Guru Śrī, Paramācārya Śrī, Parameṣṭhi Guru, Divyaugha Śrī, Siddhaugha Śrī, Mānavaugha Śrī, and again to Guru Śrī.
Then, in the southeast is the Heart-Śrī; in the northeast, the Head-Śrī; in the southwest, the Crest-Śrī; in the northwest, the Armor-Śrī;
in the center, the Three-Eye-Śrī; and in the four directions, the Weapon-Śrī.
Thus one should worship and offer libations (tarpaṇa). Then, in the triangle:
at the southeast corner, *raṃ ratiśrī*; at the northeast, *prīṃ prītiśrī*;
and at the front corner, *klīṃ manobhavaśrī*. Thus one should worship.

Then one should satisfy [the deities] to the north of that very triangle with "Drāṃ Ākarṣaṇabāṇa Śrī," to the south with "Drīṃ Drāvaṇabāṇa Śrī," and to its right with "Klīṃ Māraṇabāṇa Śrī" and "Nlūṃ."
Having worshipped and gratified Vaśīkaraṇabhāṇaśrī, who stands at its forefront, and likewise Mādavāṇaśrī, one should then,
to the north of that, worship Sauḥ Kāmaśrī and Klīṃ Manma.

One should worship and offer libations to Thaśrī at her right side; to Aiṃ Kandarpaśrī, Nlūṃ Makaradhvajaśrī in the southeast; and to Strīṃ Mīnaketuśrī [in the south] (as per folio 34a). Thereafter, one should worship in the eight *yonis* starting from the east.
Ditā, Anaṅgakusumāśrī, Anaṅgamekhalāśrī, Anaṅgamathanāśrī, Anaṅgamadanāturāśrī,
Subhagāśrī, Bhagāśrī, Bhagarū.
One should worship and offer libations to Pilīśrī and Bhagamālāśrī;
thereafter, on the eight petals starting from the east, [one worships] Aṃ Asi Tāṃ Gabhairavaśrī, Āṃ Brāhmīśrī, Iṃ Rudrabhai... [and so forth].
Ravaśrī Īṃ Māheśvarīśrī 2; Uṃ Caṇḍabhairavaśrī Ūṃ Kaumārīśrī 3; Ṛṃ Krodhabhairavaśrī Ṝṃ Vaiṣṇavīśrī 4; Ḷṃ Unmattabhairavaśrī Ḹṃ Vārāhī.
Śrī 5 Ekapālibhairava Śrī Aiṃ Māhendrī;
Śrī 6 Oṃ Bhīṣaṇabhairava Śrī Auṃ Cāmuṇḍā Śrī; 7 Aṃ Saṃhārabhairava Śrī.
