[Page 34b] One should worship and offer libations with "Aḥ Nārasiṃhī Śrī. Then, at the locations of the knots, starting from the west: "Śrī Kāmarūpa-pīṭha," "Śrī Kaulagiri-pīṭha," and so forth.
One should worship and offer libations to Lāntakapīṭhaśrī, Cauhārapīṭhaśrī, Jālandharapīṭhaśrī, Oḍiyānapīṭhaśrī, and Devakūṭapīṭhaśrī. Thus [it is said]. Ta.
From the western side of the excellent circular mandala, proceeding upwards and downwards,
[are] Herukabhairavaśrī, Vetālabhairavaśrī,
Tripurāntakabhairavaśrī, and Agnijihvabhairava.
Vaśrī Kālāntakabhairavaśrī, Kapālibhairavaśrī, Ekapādabhairavaśrī, Bhīmarūpabhairavaśrī,
Malayabhairavaśrī, Hāṭakeśvara.

One should worship and offer libations to Rabhairavaśrī; thereafter, at the four corners starting from the east, one should worship Indraśrī, Agniśrī, Yamaśrī, Nṛtiśrī, Varuṇaśrī, and Vāyuśrī. (Folio 35a)
One should worship and offer libations to Īśānaśrī between Indra and Īśāna, Brahmaśrī between Varuṇa and Rākṣasa, and Viṣṇuśrī; thereafter, one should do so in their very vicinity.
One should worship and offer libations to Vajraśrī, Śaktiśrī, Daṇḍaśrī, Khaḍgaśrī, Pāśaśrī, Dhvajaśrī, Gadāśrī, Triśūlaśrī, Padmaśrī, and Cakraśrī.
And then, in that square: Vāṃ Vaṭuka Śrī in the west; Yāṃ Yoginī Śrī in the north;
Kṣāṃ Kṣetrapāla Śrī in the east; and Gaṃ Gaṇapati Śrī in the south.
Thus one should worship and offer libations: Vasuśrī in the northwest,
the twelve Ādityas along with Śrī in the northeast, the eleven Rudras along with Śrī in the southeast, and all the Bhūtas along with Śrī in the southwest.
One should worship and offer libations.

Having thus worshipped the enclosure (āvaraṇa), and having again worshipped and gratified the root goddess within the bindu as before, and having displayed the mudrās and worshipped with three handfuls of flowers, [he should proceed].
One should perform the *tyā-homa* as follows: having drawn and visualized a wheel, a triangle, and a square in either fire or water, [one offers oblations] to Prāṇa svāhā,
Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna.

Having offered oblations with this Gāyatrī mantra, and having thus offered the six ancillary (ṣaḍaṅga) oblations, one should then offer oblations to one's own deity with the root mantra according to one's capacity; then,
having bid farewell to the spiritual friend (suhṛd), [one should proceed] to the Īśāna-maṇḍala.

Having performed [the preliminary rites], one says: "Oṃ, obeisance to Vaṭukāya! Come, come, O Lord of the Devas, O Vaṭukanātha, radiant with a mass of tawny matted locks, three-eyed, with a flaming mouth; destroy, destroy all obstacles!"

"Accept the bali offering along with all ritual services, svāhā"—thus is the *vaṭuka-bali*. To the Yoginīs in the southeast, salutation (*namaḥ*). Above, to Brahmā... [to] the Yoginī in the south... *pṛ0* 36a).

*Bhyaḥ svāhā sarvayoginī hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*— this is the offering (*bali*) for the Yoginīs. In the southwest (*naiṛta*), *kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ*, [offering] together with the *alibalih* for the Kṣetrapāla.
*Valiṃ gṛhṇa 2 svāhā*—this is the *bali* offering for the Kṣetrapāla. In the northwest: *Gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ gaṇapataye vara-varada sarvajanaṃ me vaśam ānaya baliṃ gṛhṇa 2*.
Having offered the *bali* to Gaṇapati with the mantra "Svāhā," and having likewise offered the *bali* to the goat and other animals,
one should perform meditation on the Guru and the Deity and carry out recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity.
Furthermore, O you who perform prāṇāyāma, ṛṣi-nyāsa, and so forth, and who, immediately after the nyāsa, are the protector of that which is more secret than the secret—
accept this recitation performed by us; may there be success.
O Goddess Maheśvarī, by your grace, may I [attain this].

Having thus offered the fruit of the recitation, which consists of light, into the left hand of the Goddess, and having recited the armor (*kavaca*), the thousand names (*sahasranāma*), the hymn (*stotra*), and so forth, one should perform the eight-limbed prostration (*aṣṭāṅga-pratipatti*) and circumambulate her.
Having performed the ritual salutation to the maṇḍala at the appointed time, [he recites:
"May all practitioners be happy; may all detractors perish; may my state be that of Śambhu; may the Guru be pleased."

Having recited the *Śānti* beginning with "Always" (*sadā*) and so forth, and having worshipped with the mantra "Obeisance to Nirmālyavāsinī, [the goddess] of the floral remains of the Lord" (*īśānena nirmālyena nirmālyavāsinyai namaḥ*), one should then [recite]: "Whatever [fault] was previously committed by me while waking, dreaming, or in deep sleep..."
Whatever has been spoken by me through my mind, speech, feet, belly, genitals, breath, body, and authority over dharma— all that, along with everything else, belongs to Śrī Tripurabhairavī.
"May there be surrender at your feet; Om Tat Sat.
Having thus surrendered one's own self, one should wander with a peaceful countenance. May there be auspiciousness for the Kaulas who have attained their state through his grace.
This *Bhairavī-paddhati* has been composed in brief by those belonging to various [religious] orders who have sought it from outsiders. Thus ends the *Śrī-tripurabhairavī-nityapūjā-paddhati*.
Oṃ. Now, in this *Dharmapraśnatantra*, Śrī Pārvatī spoke to Mahādeva, the God of gods, who is proficient in all scriptures: "O Lord of the World, have mercy; you are a knower of Dharma."
O Mahāmati, Suṃdarī spoke another [mantra] called the Vidyā that Fills the Three Cities; tell me truly her divine armor (kavaca). Of her—
Having heard those words, the Lord of the World spoke of the wondrous armor (*kavaca*) of the goddess, which is beautiful yet appears deformed.
Śrī Īśvara said: "Tell [it]."
Listen to this Great Knowledge Armor (Mahāvidyākavaca), which is difficult to obtain at all times.
Having heard it according to the prescribed rite, you must keep it secret; by its grace, I sustain the entire universe. (pṛ0 37ba) 4.14)
She from whom the entire three worlds have arisen and in whom they still abide; she who is honored by the world as mother and father,
whose very nature is the protection of the world, and who bestows spiritual perfection.
She who is well-established among the three, well-established among the six, and born from those who are not wicked;
she who brings benefit to all beings and is the very nature of all beings; O Goddess, protect me with the syllable *ka*, you who are the embodiment of desire and the one who grants desires.
May the goddess Dāyinī protect me; may the goddess Aiṃkārī, whose nature is the root support, protect me. May the goddess Īṃkārī, who bestows all desires, protect me; may Lakāra protect me.

May the Goddess Indrāṇī, the beloved of Indra; may the Goddess Hrīṃkārī, the beautiful consort of Śambhu, protect me everywhere. May Mahāmāyā, the consort of Śambhu, protect my head with these syllables.

The goddess Kakārīpātumām always assumes a form at will;
the goddess Kakārīpātumām is forever the beloved of Śaṃvarāri. The goddess Lakārīpātumām...

May the goddess Hrīṃkārī, who assumes the form of Rādhāraṇi and whose body is half that of Śaṅkara, protect me with these syllables; may Mahāmāyā, the beloved of Kāmarāja, protect me; may Makārī protect me.

May the goddess Sāvitrī, the bestower of all, protect me (14). May Kakārī, whose essential nature is the essence of all arts, protect me everywhere. May Lakārī, the goddess Lakṣmī, who possesses all auspicious marks, protect me.
May Hrīṃkārī protect everywhere; may the Goddess Tribhuvaneśvarī protect [me] with these syllables; may Mahāmāyā, whose nature is Śakti, protect [me]. May Vāgbhava protect the head.

May Tuvadanā, who possesses the nature of the King of Desire (Kāmarāja) and the form of Śakti, protect my heart and grant the accomplishment of mantras. May the beautiful Suṃdarī, who is red in color, always protect me. 17. May Suṃdarī always protect me. She is red in color.

May Sadāpādusuṇdarī, the giver of all things, protect [me] forever. May Suṇdarī, endowed with various ornaments, protect [me] always. May Sarvāṅgasuṇdarī, the bestower of auspiciousness everywhere, protect [me]. 18–19.
May she who generates delight for the world, whose form is that of Śambhu, who bestows meat [or flesh] at all times,
who consists of all mantras, and who grants all auspicious fortune— may that Goddess, who is composed of all Lakṣmī, grant supreme bliss. 20.
The goddess Pātumāṃsā is always the auspicious Śivā who bestows various treasures of conch-shells. Then there is the goddess Padmanidhi,

May Vāgdevī protect me always; may she who dwells everywhere protect me always (30, p. 38b). May Vaśinī protect me always; may she who bestows great siddhis protect me always.
May Sarvavidrāviṇī protect me; may Gaṇanātha protect me always.
May Goddess Durgā protect me always; may Vaṭuka protect me always; may Kṣetrapāla protect me always; may Sādhāraśaktikā protect me. 32. May Ananta protect me always.
May the Boar protect me always; may the Earth protect me always, as well as the golden lion-throne. May the red nectar and the ambrosia protect me constantly at all times. 33. Sudhā.
May the Kalpavṛkṣa tree always protect me; may it always protect me. May the white parasol always protect me; may the jewel-lamp always protect me.
May the Nandana garden constantly protect me for the sake of all accomplishments. 34–35.
May the world-protectors, Indra and the others, protect [me] always;
likewise, may their vehicles protect [me] always, and may their weapons protect [me] always.
May their armaments protect [me] always. 35. May their implements protect [me] always.
May the Pātur-yoginīs protect [me] always; may the Siddhas protect [me] always.
May the Goddess who bestows all accomplishments (siddhis) protect [me]; may she grant [them] at all times. May the Goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī protect [me] everywhere and at all times. 36.
The Goddess whose form is bliss, whose nature is consciousness, and who consists of pure awareness;
she who is beautiful everywhere, who is beautiful at her feet, and who is beautiful even in the terrible abode of separate deities. 37.
O Pārvatī, when on a mountain difficult to traverse or in a forest or wilderness,
the beautiful Śivā said, "Wear this armor," and thus the extraction of the mantra was spoken. 38–39.

Whoever, having become disciplined and pure, recites this at the three junctions of the day with self-restraint, shall achieve the fulfillment of all goals that exist within his heart. (40) [With] gorocanā and kuṅkuma...

With red sandalwood or with white flowers, [one should worship] the Self-Arisen One (Svayambhū) on a birch leaf under Saturn; or in a cremation ground, or in a wilderness, or in an empty house. (41) [Page 39b] Śmaśāne prāntare vāpi śūnyāgāre śi...

In the temple, having worshipped the yantra with incense, agallochum (agaru), and flowers, [he should worship] the young maidens (kumārikās) (42). Having worshipped their mantra, he should especially worship the lineage of gurus. He should worship...
Having given according to one's ability and having praised according to the rite prescribed by the Sage (43), one should have the *yantra* worn after the Guru has worshipped it;
and having worshipped it in the vulva of a young girl (*kumārikā*).

Likewise, having offered a row of *caguru* incense, and then having presented the oblation (*bali*) to the Goddess, one should worship with men, cats, pigs, mongooses, buffaloes, and rams according to the prescribed ritual. 44–45.

Having placed it, set within gold, upon the neck, the left [arm], or the head, on an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation at sunrise; likewise, having donned this armor (*cakravaca*), one becomes invincible in all respects. 46.147.
A man shall obtain success; yet, O Maheśānī, I am not able to describe its greatness or its fruit even in hundreds of years. It is inexhaustible.
There shall be no fear of thieves, nor there any affliction by disease;
nor shall there be fear of famine, nor any oppression whatsoever.
There shall be the pacification of all obstacles and the alleviation of all diseases.

It is destructive [of obstacles], (49) it provides all protection for living beings, and it bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. It must never be spoken of here and there, nor should it ever be given away. (50) Having received the mantra...
The wise one should worship [it] constantly according to the prescribed rite; even there, O goddess whose form is divine, this single protective mantra (kavaca) is considered difficult to obtain.
Having received the grace of the Guru and having attained the Vidyā...

Even there, one should conceal this divine armor (*kavaca*), which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds. Whoever, being restrained and pure, recites this true verse (*śloka*)—for him, all [attainments]... [52]
The accomplishment of one's purpose shall occur; this was proclaimed by Śaṅkara.
(53) Hara himself is the Guru and the God, and Pārvatī is his wife; for him who worships them without distinction, there is success.
"Success is not far off. (54) Thus ends the *Śrītripurabhairavī-kavaca* in the *Śrīviśvasāra-tantra*.
Oṃ. Now, the Thousand Names (*sahasranāma*). Oṃ. Now I shall speak.
This thousand-name hymn of the Goddess Maheśānī,
by whose grace, O Maheśānī, one may obtain the fruits of all classes [of merit],
the pacification of all diseases, and [protection from] all death.
This hymn, which brings about the destruction [of all obstacles] and bestows all peace,
was spoken by Śaṅkara; there is no hymn superior to this,
no austerity superior to this, and nothing superior to this.
O Maheśvarī, there is no higher *dyātīrtha* than this, wherein everything that has arisen remains, and at the time of dissolution, all that shall go to its dissolution.
Of this *Sahasranāmastotra-mantra* of the venerable Tripurabhairavī, the Lord Śiva is the seer (*ṛṣi*),
the *paṅkti* meter is the metre (*chandas*), and the Primordial Power (*Ādyāśakti*) is the deity (*devatā*).
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation, [addressed] to the deity Tripurabhairavī. Oṃ, O Tripurā,
Supreme Sovereign, dweller in all accomplishments...
The Goddess consisting of the Ṛgveda mantra, endowed with all powers;
the auspicious Goddess consisting of all streams, the bestower of all prosperity;
she who is the Yoginī, the Mother of Yoga, and like an ocean of yoga.
The fierce one, to be meditated upon by yogis, the mother of yogis, she who delights in the enjoyment of yoga; she who is playful sport,
as well as the manifestation of the form of time through her divine play, she whose nature is Time.
Pākālarātri, Kālī, she who dwells in the lotus, whose form is the splendor of Kamalā, the sovereign of Kāmarāja, Kriyā— why is she angry? She who possesses a deceptive guise.
Having the form of a banner and a small flag, adorned with white water-lilies,
she is the beloved Kālarātri, the locus of all activity,
possessing a terrible roar and a fearsome form that destroys the compassion of those who utter such roars.
She who always delights in the terrible roar of the swirling Ghargharāghariṇī river;
she whose form is fierce, yet more non-terrible (Aghoratarā); she who bestows the destruction of sins and heat;
she who possesses the ringing sound of bells, and is herself the bell (Ghaṇṭā).
She who is always fond of sound, subtle and subtler than the subtle,
grosser than the gross, possessed of great intelligence, patient, radiant, formidable, and the source of terrifying sounds.
She who is of incomparable form, the remover of fear, the giver of fearlessness, the destroyer of fear;
the Goddess who dwells in the cremation ground, who resides in the abode of the cremation ground, who sits upon corpses, and who carries corpses.
Dwelling within the corpses of dead bodies, carrying corpses as her food,
wearing a bracelet of human skulls around her neck, devouring teeth, truthful yet appearing untruthful, she possesses a mass of hair as dark as a swarm of bees.
She who steals away the body of falsehood, she who delights in speaking the truth, she whose abode is truth, she who is associated with truth, she who sports in truth,
she who is unattached yet well-attached, and she who is the company of the virtuous.
She who deludes through union, the mistress of illusion, the great lore, she who sports in the great intoxicant; she who takes away the wine,
she who destroys the ocean of drinking and intoxication, with blood flowing [from her].
She who dwells in the blood of the Ramālāca, who is intensely addicted to great intoxication, who moves through the noose of flesh and weapons of meat,
who subsists on flesh, who wears flesh, who is the boundary of flesh, and who devours flesh.
She who drinks blood, whose desire is for blood, whose mouth is red, whose eyes are red, whose food is blood, who is fond of blood,
who destroys the *raktanimbaka* tree, whose hands are red, and whose garments are red.
One whose body is blood-red from the *svayaṃbhū* flower,
who is eager for the *svayaṃbhū* flower, who utters the *svayaṃbhū* mantra, who is a destroyer of the *svayaṃbhū* [tree], and who is adorned with *svayaṃbhū* flowers.
She is the one who delights the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), the destroyer of the enemy,
she whose playful grace is like that of a bull, she who takes pleasure in the bull,
she who originates from the bull, and she whose essence is semen.
Kāśu, Krakarā, Suśukrā, Śukriṇī, she who is worthy of worship by those who worship Śukra, the reviler of those who revile Śukra, Raktamālyā, Raktapuṣpā, and Raktapuṣpakā.
Puṣpikā, she whose limbs are anointed with red sandalwood, who wears red sandalwood paste, the fish-like one, the beloved of the fish, the female fish,
the one who does not eat fish, the one of great prosperity, and the one who desires fish.

The destroyer of fish-eaters and those who revile fish; likewise, she is Keka-rākṣī, the fierce one who destroys cruel beings. She is Krūrā, whose body is like a thunderbolt (kuliśa), and Rājyāṅgī, [the embodiment of] sovereignty.
She is the source of all existence, possessing a vajra-body, the destroyer of the vajra, the one who bestows the vajra-skeleton,
she whose navel is deep, the remover of fear,
the one who appears as fearlessness, the remover of fear, the giver of fear, and the one who is both fearful and fearless.
She who is not terrifying, who is free from fear, who delights the mind, who is beautiful,
the mistress, the truthful, the bringer of well-being, and likewise the bringer of security;
she whose parting of the hair is honored from afar, and whose form resembles vermilion.
She whose nose is adorned with pearls, she of the beautiful nose, she of the smooth nose, she who is short, she with a protruding belly, she who is tall,
she who is terrifyingly long, she with great hair, she who is crooked, and she who is spotted.
Caṇḍī, Caṇḍanādā, Aticaṇḍikā, Aticaṇḍā, Mahācaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍaveginī, Caṇḍālī, Caṇḍikā,
and Caṇḍaśabdarūpamahābalā Caṇpā. (Folio 43b)
She who is like Campāvatī, whose conduct is pure and exceedingly sharp, who bestows victory through the union of giving, who causes joy to the world,
who is worshipped by the world, the mother of the world, and the world itself.
She who is the patience of the three worlds, the victory, the conqueror of non-victory,
the giver of victory, and the victorious one; she who is the mother, the sustainer of the world, known as Victory (Jayā), whose very form is victory, and who is honored by the universe.
Victory to the Mother of the World,
the Glory of Victory, the Bringer of Triumph, the Victorious One, the Mother of Victory, Jaya, Vijayā, Janā, Ṣaṅgī, she whose form is the sword, Suṣaṅgā, and the Holder of the Sword.
The goddess Riṇī, whose form is union, who brings about union, whose limbs are united, who is beloved by union, who bestows union, who is the illusion of union,
who possesses union, who is the circle of union, and who holds a conch and a bow.
Vajriṇī, Musulīmatī, Vāṇinī,
Ḍipālī, Pāśī, Aṅkuśīśvarī, Dhanuṣī, Taṅkinī, Carmī, Kuṇtī, and Karṇanāsī.
She who takes the form of a mallet and a plow, who dwells in the field of Halirana, who is the source of the plow, the wielder of the plow,
whose form arises from the plow, who is the peerless sport of the perfectly balanced scales, and who is beyond all comparison.
She who is beloved by the lute and the vine, who bears various weapons, who arises from divine missiles, whose form consists of the visible and the invisible,
and of gain and loss; she who is the essence of *dha*.
She who bestows the wealth of the final syllable *ni*, who assumes forms both auspicious and inauspicious, who wields the bow,
who is the sound of the word "bow," who is the measure of the bow, who supports the earth,
who is the source of the sound "Dhīra," whose names are inexhaustible, who is the giver of prosperity, and whose limbs are beautiful.
The resident of the new [abode], the giver of the wealth of Dharma,
she who is to be attained through great wealth, the great bow, she whose form is both unpeaceful and peaceful,
she who dwells on the path of the breath, and the multitude of the sky.

She is to be served; she is the beloved of the Gaṇas, the giver of the Gaṇas, the destroyer of the Gaṇas, and the one who censures the coming and going of the Āgamas. She is to be approached, yet she is free from the desire for sexual union; she is the destroyer of disease and the increaser of health. Priya.

She who is both beloved and yet to be beloved, who is dear and yet not dear to the heart; she who bestows what is dear and yet is not dear, who is established in existence, yet is well-firm, of a firm nature, and yet unstable in her giving.
She who increases steadfastness, she who is restless, she who dwells among the unsteady and the fickle women, Gaurī, Kālī, as well as Chinnā, Māyā, Yāmyā, and the one of praised splendor, Sundarī.
She who is auspicious for the three cities, who dwells in Tripurīśvara, who has the three cities as her seat, the Goddess who takes away the life of the three cities,
she who is Bhairavī, who resides in Bhairava, and who is the beloved body of Bhairava.
She who has Bhairava as her body, the terrifying one, the beloved of Bhairavī, Kālī, Kālarātri, Bhadrakālī, Pṛthivī, Āyanī, Kriyā, Krayadā, Krayahā, Kreyā, Kraya... [p. 45a]
She who is as dear as life itself is Klīṃkārī, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Śakti, Svāhā, the All-pervading One, the Sovereign, Prakṛti, and Puruṣa; she who bears masculine names and possesses a masculine form.
Puruṣāṅgī, Pūruṣī, as well as Prakṛti assuming form, the Supreme Puruṣa, and likewise Māyā-Nārāyaṇī,
Mati, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vītathā, Vārāhī, Cāmuṇḍā, Rudrāṇī,
Haravallabhā, Kauverī, Śambhavī, Kṛṣṇā, Kātyāyanī, Apūjanā, Rākṣasī, and Ḍākinī.
Nīcitrā, Vicitrā, Citrakramā, Tathāhaṃ, Sinī, Rākiṇī, Tīkṣṇā, Gāndhārī, Gandhavāhanā, Kekarī, Koṭarākṣī, Nirmāṃsā, and Sra... [the list continues].

She who bestows forgiveness, whose tongue is beautiful and well-formed, who grants a pleasing countenance, who possesses the splendor of the moon, the radiance of the moon, and the lunar light, she who is devoted to the beauty of the moon, the immortal one, the producer of nectar, and the nourisher.
Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā,
Pūrṇāmṛtā, Kalpalatikā, and Kalpavṛkṣā.
She who bestows gifts, whose hands are capable or incapable [of action], whose body brings about the end of the eon, who is named after the eon, who is both beyond the eon and auspicious,
and whose body brings about the destruction of the eon— she who is named after the eon.
Lpabhavyā, Acakalpavaṃdakā, Vaṃdakā, Śucimukhī, Pretamukhī, Ulkāmukhī, Mahāmukhī, Sumukhī, Ulūkavadanā, Kākāsyā, Vikā, and Vika.
She has the faces of a lizard and a chameleon, and the faces of a snake, a tortoise, and a sharabha; possessing various mouths and various forms,
she is the upholder of the earth, the one worshipped by the universe, and the universe itself.
The Mother known as Viśvā, the source of all existence, who abides within the solar orb; she is the splendor of the sun, the radiance of the sun, the digit of the sun, named the Sun,
and the light of the sun.
The forest [of the subtle body] consists of the channels Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci,
Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā,
Vodhinī, Dhāriṇī, Kṣamā, Yugadā, and Yugahā.
She who increases what is fit for digestion and unfit for digestion, she who resides within the fire-mandala, whose abode is the fire-mandala, the beloved of fire,
she who brings about the class of fire, she whose food is fire, she who is intensely red, and she who is within the fire.
She who is the fire of passion, the fire that destroys the forest-fire of worldly existence, the beloved of Fire, the digit of Fire,
she who dwells eternally within Fire, and whose forms are smoke-colored rays, heat, and blazing flames.

The goddess Jyotirbrahmakuṭumbinī, who possesses various splendors, whose nature is that of the celestial women emitting sparks, and who likewise consumes the *bali*, the *havya*, and the *kavya* offerings, is the Supreme Brahman.
The Goddess Haimayī is the supreme Brahman in essence; she is the Supreme Self,
the highest, the giver of merit, the increaser of merit,
auspicious by day, auspicious by name, and the kinswoman of merit.

She whose body is beloved, whose name is meritorious, who is honored for her merit, who increases the limbs of great men, whose body is auspicious, who performs meritorious deeds, who censures those who censure virtue, and who is the auspicious time itself.
She who wears a garland of both merit and demerit;
she whose character is merit yet whose play is demerit; she whose name is merit and who is equal to the Supreme; she who is served by merit and who is the ancient, subtle essence of merit.
She who is the beloved of the city, she whose life-breath is attained by men and non-men,
she whose essential nature is the Self of the Puruṣa, she whose limbs are the Puruṣa,
she who is the body dear to the Puruṣa, and she who is well-flowered.

She who possesses flowers as her life-breath, she who takes away flowers, she who is dear to flowers, she who loves flowers, she who wears garlands of flowers, she who brings joy through flowers, she who is the delight of Nandaka, she who is rich in flowers, she who is adorned with flower-garlands, and she who destroys those who revile flowers.
Rghā, Apāpā, Anāmā, Nila,
as well as Kṣattraprāṇahartrī, Mahāśaṅkhavāsinī, Sahā, Śaṅkheśvarī, Mālā, Matsyagandhā, and Mahodā.
Long-bellied, long-lipped, with long and sunken bellies;
with lips like bimba fruit, with visible noses, with long nostrils,
very long, great long, and hanging long.
Bavāhinī, Laṃvahā, Laṃvaśakti, Calamba, Sthālambapūjikā, Nirlambā, Sulambā,
Mahālambā, Durgamā, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, and Mahāghaṇṭā.
She who always delights in the sound of the ṭāṅka-bell, who loves musical instruments, who takes pleasure in music, who destroys the sound of evil instruments, who is the delight of the senses,
who possesses a most beautiful form, and who is naturally well-subdued.
She whose thighs begin with the power of subjugation, who is dear to Rāma, who makes the garden (Rāma) joyful,
whose limbs are beautiful, who is the delight of the lover,
who is beloved by Rati, who possesses passion, who is to be served by Rati, who is the pleasure of her beloved, and who is divine delight.
Kurati is beauty, the destroyer of both auspicious and inauspicious;
she is supreme beauty, great beauty, exceeding beauty, and exquisite beauty;
she is the alluring one, great longing, beautiful longing, and the beginningless longing.

The increasers of existence, those whose limbs are greed, those who perceive greed as their intellect, those who are not greedy, the destroyers of greed, those who delight in greed, the great greed itself,
the revilers of those who revile greed, and the dwellers within the limbs of greed.

She who possesses a dark fragrance, who is free from odor, who destroys all foul smells, who is the fragrance of Gāndhārī, who is worshipped for her scent, who is sweetly fragrant, whose fragrance is love, who has a difficult-to-attain scent, who is pure fragrance, who is exceedingly fragrant, and who is the very essence of fragrance.
Mahāgandhā, Asragandhā, Arhagandhā, Gandhanāśakanāśinī, Padmā, Padmāvatī, Premā, Padmagandhā, Sugandhikā, Padmālayā, Padmakarā, and Padmavāsinī.

She whose vehicle is a swan, who dwells upon a lotus, whose face is like a lotus, who sports with the lotus, who possesses a beautiful fire, who is the end of the lotus, who carries the lotus, who is the benefactress of the lotus-palace, and who censures those who revile the lotus.
The goddess whose vehicle is contentment with the four lotuses, who holds a red utpala,
who is ever fond of the red utpala,
who possesses the fine fragrance of the red utpala, and who dwells within the red utpala.
She whose garden-houses are red lotuses, who is captivating with her red lotuses,
whose eyes are like beautiful red lotuses, who assumes the form of a red lotus, and who is the woman, Nārāyaṇī, and Īśānā.
The beloved of Nārāyaṇa’s abode, the one who captivates the heart of Nārāyaṇa while dwelling within his body, she who is saluted by Nārāyaṇa— Nārāyaṇī.
Born from the limbs [of Nārāyaṇa], she is the beloved body of Nārāyaṇa; she is Vaiṣṇavī, worshipped by Viṣṇu, and her body is established as Vaiṣṇavī.
She is worshipped by Hara, the most excellent of Hara’s [consorts], the imperishable beloved of Hara.
She is intent on the withdrawal, the ascent, the abiding in the body, and the worship of Hara;
she has emerged from the body of Hara and dwells within the limbs of Hara;
she is worshipped by the worshippers of Hara and is ever devoted to the delight of Hara.
Mounted upon the body of Śiva, she delights in the play of Hara with his consort;
she is well-joined yet free from conflict, unattached and the destroyer of attachment; she is the invincible fortress of solitude, increasing within the difficult-to-traverse body.
She who dwells in the fortress, whose form is the fortress, who increases the body of the fortress, who is the end of the body of the fortress, whose form is the fortress, who removes misfortune,
who is dear to the spirits (pretas), who creates the spirits, and who is the spirit of the dead.
Born from laughter, dwelling in the bodies of pretas,
she crushes the bodies of pretas and other spirits; she is the Ḍākinī, the Yoginī, the embodiment of the goddess, ever fond of Kālarātri, and the destroyer of Kālarātri.

She whose body is dark as time, possessing a great form yet slender-limbed; she with limbs like a thunderbolt, with a vajra-body, assuming the form of a vajra; the blessed one who assumes various bodies, dwelling in the sequence of the six chakras.
Residing in the *mūlādhāra*, she is always situated in the *mūlādhāra*; she is Mahāmāyā in the form of wind, dwelling on the path of the wind,
endowed with wind, creating wind, and filled with wind.
She who fills the body with blood, she who assumes the form of the vital breath (*vāyu*), she who moves through the path of the *suṣumnā*, she who resides within the body yet is beyond the body,
she who is to be meditated upon as the body yet is bodiless, she who has the form of the channels (*nāḍī*) yet is not a channel.
Sthānavī, Nalinānanā, Iḍā, Piṅgalā,
Suṣumnā, and Sarasvatī— these are the forms of Mūlaprakṛti who constantly bring delight to Sadāśiva and consist of nectar.
She who dwells within the limbs of the adornment of Maheśāna (the Great Lord), she who is the creator, sustainer, and destroyer, she who resides in the state of dissolution,
she who is joined with the great dissolution, and [she who is] creation and destruction.
She who performs sacrificial acts, she who is Svadhā and Svāhā, the carrier of oblations, the beloved of oblations, ever delighting in oblations, the abode of oblations, the consumer of oblations,
born from the body of the oblation, and she whose play consists of the oblation.

Surabhi, who arises from the form and formlessness of the wish-fulfilling cow, is auspicious, the mother of the cows, the constituent part of sacrifice, beloved of sacrifice, established in sacrifice,
the body of sacrifice, the Yoginī, and the bearer of the womb.

The one born not from a womb, the truthful Satī, the untruthful Asatī, the one whose body was shattered by her husband’s curse; she who went to Ahalya’s husband, the one who should not have been approached, the destroyer of the body through grief, and the daughter-in-law of Gāndhārī and Draupadī.
Tīśivādūtī, Śivapriyā, Tripureśī,
Pañcadaśī, Paurṇamāsī, Caturdaśī, Pañcamī, as well as Ṣaṣṭhī, Navamī, Aṣṭamī, and likewise Ekā.

She who bestows fearlessness in the form of the tenth and twelfth lunar days, who is the nature of the *saṃkrānti*, who takes the form of the months, who is the embodiment of the seasons and is fond of the seasons,
who is the primordial Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and who assumes the forms of the *ghaṭikā* and the *daṇḍa*.
She who is Yamarūpā Mahākālī, the destroyer of the union with Saṃdhyā; she who is Triyāmā, Amārūpā, Yamakanyā, Yamī, Yamā, and Kularūpā Mātaṅgī.
She who destroys both noble and ignoble lineages, the beloved of the family,
she who is slender yet increases the body of the jar-like [elephant], she who is swift, the multitude of the clan, the one who moves with haste, she of ruddy luster, the river, the ocean.
She is the pacification of passion, the form of peace, the most auspicious bringer of tranquility;
she dwells within the forms of desire, thirst, hunger, agitation, and non-agitation; she is the river Śā, the house of peace, and sacred revelation.

She is mindfulness, the earth, the ground, day and night, the body composed of the five elements, and the one who possesses a beautiful form; she is the lineage of the Kurus, the one whose limbs are severed, the one who wears the serpent as her sacred thread, and the one who possesses the [four] castes.
The ḍākinī-śaktis are Kurukullā, Sukullikā,
Aparājitā, Pratyagīrā, Ajitā, Jayanāśanī, and Jayā.
And she who is thus the slayer of Mahiṣāsura, the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the annihilator of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the killer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, and the beloved of Raktavīja—
She who is the elephant, the glory of Kāśī, the abode of Kāśī, the bearer of the burden, Pārvatī, the supreme Aparṇā, the goddess Caṇḍikā, Mṛḍānī, Ambikā, and the digit of Śuklā.
Rukmiṇī and Rādhikā, whose forms are like the crescent of the autumnal moon and who possess black and red complexions,
are proclaimed as Bhairavī. 1000 Oṃ Aṣṭā.
By the recitation of the names of one thousand one hundred goddesses,
ten million great sins (*mahāpātaka*) as well as secondary sins (*upapātaka*) shall be dissolved; by this hymn held [in mind], everything is destroyed.
Whether reciting the whole or even a single verse, whether remembering it or reciting it aloud, or even causing others to recite it, one shall be instantly liberated from bondage at that very moment.
O Maheshvari, when there is fear at the king's gate, in a difficult pass, in a mountain stronghold,
on a mountain, or even upon a boat; or when fear has arisen from the danger of fire, or from lions and tigers— [in all these cases, we take refuge in You].
Recited amidst the turmoil of fear, this [mantra] destroys all the perils of mortals;
one without a son obtains a son, and the poor man shall obtain wealth; it is the master of all scriptures.
A physician shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices; a speaker shall become mute and a superior man shall become a servant of the king;
one should write this hymn with *gorocanā* and saffron.

One whose mind is not distracted, whether by the Guru or by Vaiṣṇavas, shall obtain the fruit of all siddhis; having worn [the mark] placed in the center of gold, one shall then obtain all desires. A woman, by wearing it on her left arm...
O Maheśvarī, for men, [this should be done] with the left hand; on a Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, or even on a Saturday,
one shall obtain the fruit of all accomplishments, provided it is performed in the early morning.
The preceptor should diligently draw [the mandala] at night in a cremation ground, or at midnight in an empty dwelling or house; however,
having seen or touched a menstruating woman, he should not draw it.
Having carefully drawn [the deity] with white, fragrant flowers and with sandalwood paste moistened with the essence of musk,
one who has thus drawn him attains [his goal].

With single-minded devotion, having worshipped the Kumārīs and especially the noble women with excellent flowers, perfumes, sandalwood, garments, and vermilion, one attains the sovereignty of the three worlds.
One should worship with seasonal flowers through the yoga of devotion; furthermore,
one should worship the goddesses or young maidens until the twelfth day,
and he shall obtain all desired fruits at that very moment.

Furthermore, there is no dependence here on established entities and the like, nor is there any refutation of opponents, nor any excessive effort that causes weariness; rather, it is thus at all times and in every moment.
One should offer an oblation measuring six thousand units and worship Śivā daily with such offerings;
one should present the oblation day and night with white flowers grown spontaneously.
One should worship the goddess Pārvatī, Bhairavī, who is accompanied by Tripurā;
one should daily feed ten or twelve Brahmins; and he who recites this three times [daily] for one month—

By this method of meditation, one who is childless shall obtain a son; by this rite, within two months, or likewise within three months, one shall become wealthy and possess great riches; and by performing it, one shall attain sovereignty.

In the same way, during the fourth month, one is liberated from long-standing disease; in the fifth month, one becomes a sovereign ruler; and in the sixth month, one obtains all prosperity; likewise, in the seventh month.
In the eighth [year], one attains the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva) and becomes a lord of speech;
in the ninth, all perfections (sarvasiddhi) arise; in the tenth, one is honored by the world;
in the eleventh, one gains mastery over kings; and in the twelfth, one becomes a Indra among men (bhūpurandara).
Whoever recites it even once shall obtain the fruit of worship; likewise,
he who, being self-restrained and pure, recites even a single verse correctly, obtains the fruit of worship.

O Maheśvarī, it was spoken by the terrifying [deity]; it is especially auspicious for the yoga of joy, for the brahmins, for the yoga of the attainment of good fortune, and for prosperity— thus the five.
O Goddess, wherever one abides—whether on Mount Myāṃva, Tathāṣaṣṭha, or anywhere else—there shall be no doubt, nor any defect such as that of the *mātrās*.
What else need be said? [She grants] all desired fruits.
"May one obtain [this]," thus ends the *Śrī Tripurabhairavī Sahasranāmastotra* in the *Śrī Viśvasāra Tantra*. It is complete and auspicious.

Oṃ, now the King of Hymns: Oṃ! Even Brahmā and the other gods do not know her subtle form, whose primordial body is the beginning of the universe; therefore, we [worship] her who has entered the breast.
We praise her who has the luster of your saffron,
whose form is the entirety of all speech, who possesses the radiance of a thousand suns suddenly arisen, and who holds the rosary of knowledge.

We worship you, Tripura, whose hands bear the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, whose lotus-face is adorned with three blue-lotus eyes, and who is encircled by the weight of a necklace of skulls—[you] possessing the luster of a stream of vermilion. 2.
Siṃdūrapūraruci... pṛ0 53ba).

Do those of dull intellect realize Your true nature— which is bowed down by the burden of a *raṅkucha* fruit, attainable only through the fruit of merit accumulated in other births, and yet agitated by mutual divisions, quarrels, and differences of opinion?
O Mother of the worlds, some sages call you the gross,
while others, proficient in the Vedas, call you the subtle; others say you are the abode of speech, and yet others declare you to be the root of all existence.
We consider you to be an ocean of boundless compassion;
we meditate upon you within our hearts— you who are adorned with the moon as a crest-jewel, as white as an autumnal cloud, and consisting of fifty syllables.

[She is] three-eyed, holding in her lotus-hands a rosary, a jar filled with nectar, and a book; Śambhu has half his body joined by you, the daughter of the mountain, and Viṣṇu [is likewise]. 5. You... me.
Your body is encircled by a garland of lotuses; you are the one born from the lotus (Brahmā).

You are the ground of the dwelling of Śivā’s speech, and you alone are the activity and the movement of those [beings] in Tripura. Having resorted to the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable]... pṛ0 54a) ... [you are the source].

When shall I ever behold you, the Supreme Deity, who consists of pure consciousness, who joyfully bestows the four states— waking and the others— upon the stages [of the body], and who is perceived through the senses such as the ears?
I do not forget:
having conquered the six groups of enemies, they gaze at the tip of their noses with unwavering vision and meditate upon the *ākuñcyavāyu* (the constricted vital breath).

Your form, which is adorned with the crescent moon of the waxing phase and is the friend of the rising sun, has been fashioned by the Creator; having obtained you as the half-portion of the body of the Enemy of Manmatha (Śiva), he performed his act of creation.
The Vedic declaration that "the three worlds are [Thine]" is the truth; O Mother of the world, if it were otherwise, there would be no stability for the entire universe. 9. [Regarding] worship...
On your throne,
amidst the golden peaks of Mount Meru, the wives of the Siddhas, having tasted the finest wine, sing together with the Kinnarīs beneath the celestial trees blooming with flowers.
With lotus-eyes reddened by the glow of dawn, her body possessing the playful brilliance of lightning,
she was proceeding from her own dwelling toward the royal capital of Śiva, bringing with her the very path of beauty.

One should worship the Supreme Goddess, who causes the lotus to bloom, whose limbs are sprinkled with the nectar of immortality, who is the birthplace of all births from time immemorial, and who is the consciousness of the Vedas. 11.
Ājanma... janmabhavanaṃ bhavanaṃ śrutīnāṃ caitanya-mā... [The text continues].

I take refuge in her whose lotus feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu, the source of good fortune, the abode of birth, and who dwells in Tripura exactly as she is. 12. [The meaning of the words: *Tra* means "three. *Tanu* means "body. *Maṃ* means "measure" or "extent. *Va* means "and. *Ta* means "you. *Āśrayāmi* means "I take refuge in. *Vrahmeśaviṣṇubhiḥ* means "by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu. *Upāsitapādapadmām* means "whose lotus feet are worshipped. *Saubhāgyajanmavasatim* means "the dwelling place of the origin of good fortune. *Tripure* means "in Tripura. *Yathāvat* means "exactly as she is. 12. [End of] word-meaning.
She who takes the form of the Moon creates the future world;
she sustains it again by her own power in the form of the Sun; and as the nature of Fire, she withdraws all that into Herself at the end of the age—that Śāradā.
I never forget her who is Manasija (the mind-born god),
Nārāyaṇī, the one who carries across the ocean of hell, Gaurī, the dispeller of distress, Sarasvatī, and the bestower of knowledge.

O Mother of the World, those wise ones who praise you with these twelve verses in succession, adorned by the three eyes and the three folds [of skin], become like the King of Mountains (Himavat) himself.
14. Those who praise you, the Mother of the World, with these twelve verses in order, following after you...
Having attained perfection in speech, they shall obtain supreme prosperity. Thus ends the auspicious hymn, the fifth limb of the venerable Tripurabhairavī; may there be well-being.
